To effectively train models on code-switched data, a significant amount of relevant training data is crucial, particularly when it comes to rare code-switched sequences. Enhancing this requirement has led to the development of data augmentation methods aimed at generating new examples to supplement existing datasets. Existing code-switched data augmentation methods primarily rely on deleting or replacing segments from existing examples. Notably, there has been a lack of investigation into methods that can generate new code-switched sequences. This research aims to address this gap by exploring the application of a novel data augmentation method called lexical substitution to generate new code-switched sequences. This approach involves replacing words in existing code-switched sequences with alternative words from parallel corpora, utilizing word embeddings as a reference. Our findings indicate that a substantial 90% decrease in word substitutions results in improved performance across various evaluation metrics. Furthermore, when combined with existing code-switching models, our developed code-switching models significantly outperform baseline models on English-Arabic and Arabic-English data sets in terms of BLEU scores, with notable improvements ranging from 1.8 to 4.3. This research not only contributes to the development of code-switching models but also provides valuable insights for developers to enhance data augmentation methods, particularly in contexts with limited data availability. In reinforcement learning environments, continuity of the future reward function is often assumed. However, ensuring this condition in real-world applications where rewards are defined in complex metric spaces can be problematic. This paper proposes an relaxation of the continuity condition, allowing future reward functions to exhibit "almost" continuous behavior with diminishing errors as rewards converge. Building upon this concept, we demonstrate that $G$-continuity, our proposed relaxation, suffices to establish the continuity of the value function. This result enables non-measurable state or action spaces to be effectively handled through coarse-grained analysis. To validate our approach, we employed a coarse-grained dynamic programming algorithm, proving its almost-optimality under our proposed $G$-continuity condition. This method outperformed traditional reinforcement learning algorithms on both synthetic and real-world datasets. by releasing toxic emissions, destroying property and lives, and endangering
people's health. Wildfire toxicity is particularly hazardous due to the
toxic compounds released, which can have devastating effects on human health and
the environment. To better understand and manage this risk, we analyze past
wildfire toxicity patterns using statistical methods, enabling accurate
prediction and forecasting capabilities which can aid public health and
environmental management. By applying our model, we demonstrate improved
prediction accuracy compared to a baseline forecasting method, ultimately
resulting in better prevention and mitigation strategies for the hazardous
consequences of wildfires. The source code and data used for this research are
available for further exploration. A user-friendly web application enables real-
time forecasting and facilitates public health and environmental monitoring. 
Ultimately, our work aims to enhance wildfire management and public health
forecasting.

We compare various forms of metrically defined complexity in language and evaluate their connections. We analyzed 14 languages with 7 distinct methods of measuring sentence complexity, as well as several additional metrics including type and token density, word frequency, and other characteristics. We found significant correlations among some of these measures, but others were insignificant. We also found that some of these measures correlated with aspects of morphological complexity, such as word frequency and categorization. However, we discovered that morphological complexity does not necessarily influence syntactic complexity as suggested by Greenberg's Universal 28. Instead, we found that morphological characteristics can affect the results of complexity measures, highlighting the need for corpus-based measures of language characteristics to be validated against multiple forms of evidence. Ultimately, our study indicates that different complexity measures capture distinct aspects of language and should not be used interchangeably. They should be understood as indicators of different aspects of language rather than a single, unified property. We also suggest that future research investigate the potential relationships between these measures and additional language characteristics. Such investigations could reveal whether these measures are associated with specific patterns of development, such as language typology, and could also provide insights into potential biases in language design. By acknowledging the distinct aspects of language that these measures capture, we can avoid conflating them and gain a more nuanced understanding of their significance. Our study also provides a foundation for further research into the relationships between these measures and additional language characteristics. To test this theory, a new study examines whether self-interacting dark matter could also explain the phenomenon of weak gravitational lensing in galaxy clusters.  By analyzing data from the Coma and Perseus clusters, the researchers found no evidence that self-interacting dark matter affects weak gravitational lensing.  However, the data imposed stricter limits on how much self-interaction occurs in dark matter, specifically less than 1% for a specific type of interaction.  These limits are significantly stronger than previous estimates, suggesting that self-interacting dark matter may not be the best explanation for either galaxy collisions or weak gravitational lensing.  Furthermore, the results indicate that small-scale gravitational lensing effects, like in the case of a quadruple image of a background galaxy in the Perseus cluster, can still be fully explained by the general theory of relativity without requiring additional exotic physics.  These findings support the idea that self-interacting dark matter is not a necessary component in physics, at least not when considering the specific case of small-scale gravitational lensing effects. This paper introduces a technique for simplifying complex models by reducing their formal representation. The proposed method accommodates a range of observation methods, including both state-based and event-driven approaches. By leveraging these observations, model states can be progressively determined, enabling the identification of a simplified model that aligns with these states. This simplified model can then serve as a knowledge base, facilitating its integration into B, a tool used for logical analysis. Additionally, the paper outlines a general approach for converting discrete models representing time-based constraints into their universal representation, known as monadic second-order logic. This technique can be utilized independently or in conjunction with model simplification to achieve comparable results. To support these concepts, we have developed a prototype implementation called HFlow, which is based on the existing tool B and has been adapted with the model simplification feature. This prototype demonstrates the feasibility of these ideas through a series of practical examples. A comprehensive evaluation is also presented, comparing the resulting simplified models to those obtained through evolutionary computation methods. Notably, our results indicate that the use of observations leads to significantly smaller and more manageable models, especially when dealing with event traces, when compared to models based on state observations. Importantly, the obtained models are consistently correct, unlike the often-inaccurate models produced by evolutionary computation. This accuracy, combined with the use of complete and sound observation methods, ensures that our models are free from contradictions. Overall, the use of observations enables the generation of highly accurate and compact models, representing a major breakthrough in the field. This work is expected to have a significant impact on the development of formal verification techniques. As a future direction, we intend to extend the scope of our approach to accommodate probabilistic models. Specifically, we aim to develop a probabilistic version of the model simplification feature, allowing the identification of a simplified model that aligns with partial observations made at a probabilistic level. This development will lay the groundwork for the creation of a probabilistic version of HFlow. Moreover, the proposed technique can be leveraged in conjunction with model checking methods to support full model reduction. This combination of model simplification and model checking methods will enable the identification of a minimal model that aligns with all states identified through complete analysis. Consequently, the use of model simplification in conjunction with model checking methods will facilitate the generation of a minimal model. We analyze a class of elliptic equations where the diffusion coefficient is positive, coupled with a nonnegative, bounded, and weakly differentiable measure defined on the boundary of a domain Ω. This framework assumes a zero boundary Neumann condition and a zero integral of the measure on the boundary. Under specific smallness and regularity constraints on the diffusion coefficient and the measure, we prove the local and classical well-posedness of the associated boundary-value problem for measures supported on sets of positive dimension. Moreover, we establish the well-posedness of the same boundary-value problem for measures supported on one-dimensional sets under even more general conditions. This work draws upon ideas from the theory of Stokes equations and reflects on its connections with recent findings, particularly regarding the determination of surface energies by varifold methods. Lastly, we explore the asymptotic behavior of solutions as the measure vanishes and discuss its implications in this context. Additionally, we provide two specific applications: a regularity result concerning measures supported on one-dimensional sets with vanishing regularity at the boundary, and an analysis of a free-boundary problem involving a free surface described by a measure supported on a level set. These applications are rooted in a variational context related to a recent result by Junho Calatroni. Finally, further research directions are proposed. The content of this work was initially presented at conferences in 2020 and 2021. Moreover, relevant findings were shared during seminars at the University of Pisa in 2020 and at the University of Brescia in 2021. We investigate the connection between the guidance of quantum systems and the negativity of the Wigner function within the context of the Pauli principle. It's demonstrated that distributions lacking Wigner negativity in three dimensions cannot fulfill the requirements of the Pauli principle. However, this is not the case in lower dimensions, where Wigner negativity can still comply with the Pauli principle. Building on this understanding, we propose a measure of quantum guidance based on Wigner negativity and examine its behavior in systems involving fermions. This investigation provides insight into the characteristics of quantum systems governed by the Pauli principle. Moreover, we discuss how our findings are relevant to guiding quantum guide equations for bosons and fermions. We derive a condition ensuring that solutions to these equations exhibit Wigner negativity. This research not only delves into the fundamental aspects of quantum mechanics but also contributes to the development of quantum guidance models. Continuous-phase modulation (CPM) is a highly regarded signal format due to its robustness and simplicity in non-coherent transmission scenarios, where the receiver only requires a correlator to recover the signal. However, CPM's performance in this context comes at the expense of increased computational delay as the signal period shortens. In this paper, we investigate the added complexity resulting from CPM's non-coherent differential detection and derive a direct expression for the associated computation overhead. Building on this finding, we identify a method to minimize this additional delay by inserting a predefined sampling pattern at the CPM's symbol period, which in turn enables us to develop an efficient sampling schedule with reduced implementation loss. Our proposed schedule is further compared to the CPM's natural sampling pattern in terms of computation delay and implementation loss, which are found to be inversely correlated. Lastly, we illustrate how our proposed solutions can be applied to various CPM formats without modification. All simulations in this paper are conducted using the NumPy and PyTic libraries. The results show that our proposed sampling schedule can shorten the delay by approximately 25% for the CPM-2P format and 50% for the CPM-4P format, which is nearly noise-agnostic. These findings suggest that our proposed solutions can effectively mitigate the added complexity resulting from CPM's non-coherent differential detection with minimal impact on performance. Overall, our work provides a practical approach to reducing the delay in CPM-based systems, which is particularly beneficial in real-time applications where the CPM period is short. Recent breakthroughs in dialogue systems have been achieved through pre-training with task-agnostic large-language-models.  Despite positive outcomes, there are valid concerns about the robustness of models that rely on task-specific fine-tuning and the feasibility of developing highly specialized models for every dialogue task.  To address these limitations, we propose a pre-training strategy that is based on the meaning of dialogue.  By leveraging the meaning of dialogue, our approach can effectively capture dialogue understanding and relevance for various dialogue tasks and also be applied across multiple language domains.  Furthermore, meaning-based pre-trained models can be leveraged in various dialogue applications such as conversational question answering, conversational summarization, and other tasks.  To implement this idea, we developed the DialoGLUE benchmark and a meaning-based pre-trained model called MB-MALEVA.  Through comprehensive experiments, we demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach and achieved state-of-the-art results on the DialoGLUE benchmark while also achieving significant cost reductions.  Moreover, our model's performance on downstream tasks far surpasses that of other models, and our results also indicate that MB-MALEVA achieves highly parallelizable computations during the training and inference phases.  To facilitate the use of our model, we released the code and the DialoGLUE benchmark on the GitHub platform.  Additionally, we also released the MALEVA model used in our research on the GitHub platform.  Our research and findings have the potential to positively impact the development of highly sophisticated dialogue systems.  We believe that our work can contribute to future advancements in this area. The shift towards using language as the primary interface for human interaction has led to significant advancements in NLP driven by advances in neural networks. However, there remains a pressing need to develop more sophisticated AI capable of understanding everyday conversations. To bridge this gap, commonplace knowledge graphs like ATOMIC, which detail everyday knowledge fragmented into discrete components called commonlets, are crucial. COMET-ATOMIC 2020 marks the third installment in a series of competitions that bring together NLP and graph machine learning experts to tackle challenges in creating, querying, and learning such complex graphs. This year's edition introduces new tasks designed to enhance commonlet extraction and relationship discovery between actions and their sensory observations. A notable update from the previous series is the incorporation of symbolic methods to improve extraction efficiency and evaluation metrics that assess AI systems' ability to generate valid commonlets and commonlet chains. A total of 16 teams participated in the competition, with top performers including End-to-End Module Network, FastIE, and GEM$^{2}$, which demonstrated exceptional performance across various tasks. Detailed analysis of the results reveals that combining the efforts of symbolic and neural networks is key to achieving optimal results. Moreover, extracting and utilizing commonlets is crucial for generating accurate commonlet chains. The competition's findings and resulting models are now publicly available to the community, which serves as a valuable resource for further research and development. We present a comprehensive analysis of the data reduction pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey. Leveraging the SPIRE Herschel data, the pipeline accurately replicates the observing process and efficiently processes 8,000 raw scan maps within 24 hours. It effectively handles and combines 12 levels of reduction pipeline outputs to create 4 fully calibrated Hi-GAL product maps, including dust continuum, spectral line, and image products. These high-quality products are promptly available for scientific research, while additionally facilitating data analysis and calibration verification through a user-friendly interface. Furthermore, we detail the pipeline's expected performance in terms of noise correlation, and demonstrate its capabilities to reproduce the observed noise characteristics in all four Hi-GAL product maps. Finally, we showcase the pipeline's ability to reproduce the noise characteristics in a fully processed map of the "Bird" test region. Higher-level products such as source catalogues, cubes, and maps are generated through supplementary processing steps, and will be made available in a future phase. These include source catalogues produced via the APENSAH pipeline, and full spectral and spatial data products generated via the HSA pipeline. The Hi-GAL data reduction pipeline is publicly available under an Open Source license at https://github.com/hi-gal-dr1/hi-gal_dr1.git. To standardize TCM predictions for proton-proton collisions data analysis, we utilize the QCD equation of state (EoS) derived from lattice quantum chromodynamics for both thermal mass corrections and freeze-out conditions. The TCM is adapted to account for higher-order corrections in line with perturbative QCD, and a procedure is established to determine the EoS-based temperature shift from hadronization parameters. Our results indicate that as impact parameters increase, the EoS introduces notable changes to the TCM. Additionally, a comparison between the EoS-based and TCM initial conditions shows that the former is essential for accurately determining the normalization factor. Specifically, an enhanced factor is observed when using the EoS-based procedure compared to the TCM, with differences ranging from 2% at central pseudorapidity to 10% at high impact parameters for multiplicity estimates. The EoS-based and TCM predictions exhibit similar accuracy in describing the charged particle multiplicity distribution. However, the EoS-based procedure demonstrates improved agreement with experimental data on mean transverse momentum. Notably, the EoS-based predictions for anisotropic flow parameters show improved alignment with experimental data, with the discrepancies reduced by a factor ranging from 20% for $\varepsilons(2)$ to 50% for $\vete(4)$ in comparison to the TCM. The observed enhancements in flow parameters agreement are accompanied by a decline in predicted medium modification of identified particle yields, with the EoS-based procedure exhibiting lower values for the yield modification factor and the nuclear modification factor. The results suggest that incorporating the QCD equation of state into the TCM can lead to substantial improvements in its predictive capabilities. Future studies should focus on incorporating the EoS into the two-phase model for a more comprehensive understanding. The implementation of the EoS-based procedure for heavy-ion collisions is expected to yield similar outcomes, with the current results serving as a valuable starting point for such an extension. Furthermore, the proposed method can be adapted for use in machine learning algorithms, enabling the construction of a self-supervising TCM model. The study's findings and code are publicly accessible at https://github.com/DeepTCM/QCD-EoS-PP-pyhf. The research's outcomes support the concept of utilizing perturbative QCD in thermodynamics for TCM improvements. Additionally, the results demonstrate the potential of the TCM to model the hadronization phase in line with lattice QCD, with the EoS-based procedure covering both the parton and hadron phases

This research delves into the development of distributed optimization techniques for node placement and weight configuration problems within graph-based systems, focusing on leveraging graph filters for efficient solution strategies. Graph filters possess inherent properties that facilitate direct involvement in these problems, unlike other distributed computation methods. By utilizing sparse multiplication and shift-invariance properties, we can derive concise and effective algebraic formulations for each issue. Furthermore, we can reduce the computational complexity of suboptimal solutions derived from these formulations, and when relevant, also optimize special cases. Additionally, we can apply an additional layer of sparsity to the solutions, if required, in order to enhance their practical implementation. Our proposed methods are validated through numerical experiments and analyzed in terms of their stability, with some offering advantages over existing distributed management strategies. These methods are particularly suited to large networks due to their reduced computational and communication requirements. As a result, we can achieve linear convergence rates without the need for additional communication steps after network initialization. Notably, we can achieve this without compromising the optimality of the solutions, even in complex scenarios. The presented methods are versatile and can be applied to a broader range of problems beyond the scope of this research, with specific examples including the design of distributed control systems and the management of active networks. This study is expected to provide valuable insights for researchers working with graph filters and the fields of distributed optimization, graph signal processing, and network communications. The methods presented can be directly implemented using standard graph filter frameworks, such as the NuFFT library, and are expected to contribute positively to the growing literature on graph filter research. A dedicated website has been established to provide supplementary information, including precomputed solutions, enabling the reproduction of our research findings. This website can be accessed at https://graph-filters.github.io/distributed-management/. Lastly, all of the code and datasets utilized in this research have been made publicly available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/graph-filters/distributed-management. The physical layer of 5G mobile networks is now a major target for security attacks, with significant physical consequences and exposure to illicit data transmission over the airwaves. As a result, there is an increased need to develop secure physical layer access control systems. To address this, a new method called keyless authentication (KL) is proposed, allowing devices to verify one another without relying on shared secret keys. KL uses one-way authentication codes generated from received signals, ensuring that these codes can only be reliably decoded at the intended destination. We present a KL system designed for additive white Gaussian noise channels and demonstrate its feasibility by building a prototype using a USRP device. Experimental results confirm that KL provides robust protection against adversarial interference, including jamming attacks, while also showcasing its advantages in terms of efficiency and user experience compared to traditional key-based authentication systems. Furthermore, KL's security benefits can be enhanced through the incorporation of one-way hash functions, offering a highly secure solution for 5G mobile networks. To this end, KL is well-positioned to become a crucial component in the security architecture of future wireless systems. With its versatility, KL can be easily integrated into existing wireless standards, such as LTE and 5G, making it a practical solution for securing mobile communications in the near future. Our proposed framework, FGNET-RH, achieves improved accuracy in fine-grained named entity detection by leveraging a Poincar\'e hyperbolic model and a Refine in Hyperbolic enabled Transformer (RH-Transformer). This model capitalizes on the hierarchical relationships between entities to facilitate faster convergence and finer predictions. As entities are organized in a tree-structured taxonomy, more distant entities can be better distinguished based on their relative position in the taxonomy graph. Our FGNET-RH approach refines entity representations by incorporating graph information, ultimately producing more precise outputs. Our experiments demonstrate that incorporating refining mechanisms and taking advantage of hyperbolic space yield significant performance gains over baseline models. Crowdsourced image datasets are often marred by errors resulting from inconsistent and ambiguous label inputs, a problem compounded when pre-existing ground truth data are compromised by subsequent crowdsourcing attempts aimed at validation. This investigation seeks to address this challenge by examining the effects of labeling noise on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and proposing a novel method for evaluating and quantifying uncertainty in datasets contaminated with noisy labels. This approach involves utilizing noisy measurements of the classification probability for each class of every image in the dataset, known as 'human softmax' distributions. A key innovation of this technique is the application of maximum entropy to re-estimate the classification probabilities, effectively identifying high-uncertainty cases. Ensemble modeling is then used to refine these estimates, resulting in cleaner ground truth data which can be employed for CNN retraining. Experimental findings indicate that this method is capable of mitigating the adverse impact of labeling noise and even predictively identify noisy inputs at a reasonable false positive rate. In various fields such as customer service, education, and training, the ability of humans to adapt interlocutors' communication patterns is a vital aspect of effective communication. Entrainment facilitates interpersonal connections and maintains their maintenance are key indicators of a system's or robot's social competence. Measuring entrainment, however, is a complex task, especially in unsupervised settings. This study aims to establish a quantitative entrainment metric from spoken dialogue by comparing the similarity of speech patterns in speaker pairs. By using deep neural networks to model speaker characteristics, we distinguish genuine pairs - those exhibiting entrained speech - from non-conversational individuals speaking randomly. Our findings show that speaker pairs exhibit a statistically significant similarity advantage of over 5% when compared to random speakers, based on a comprehensive human evaluation of the similarity of their speech patterns. This study sets the groundwork for an unsupervised entrainment metric, paving the way for social dialogue system design and development. Moving forward, we plan to enhance this metric using multiple dialogue model training approaches, including self-supervised and reinforcement learning, to create more robust entrainment indicators. This work has significant implications for the development of interactive systems capable of producing natural, engaging conversations. Such systems will not only demonstrate entrained speech patterns, but also exhibit a deep understanding of their interlocutors' unique communication preferences. Ultimately, this will lead to the creation of social agents capable of forming genuine interpersonal connections. This work has been successfully showcased in a conversational demo at the IJCAI-21 conference. This paper presents an unsupervised model for identifying sequential activities within unlabelled videos. A novel self-supervised learning approach relies on the capture of temporal relationships between adjacent frames and segments to determine probable action transitions. In contrast to previous methods focusing on single predicates, our method also captures inter-frame relationships to infer co-occurring actions and their relative timing. A self-supervised learning framework extracts dense motion and activity cues from video sequences. Trained only on video data, our method segments frames into coherent actions, and a novel self-supervised aggregation scheme groups similar actions into distinct categories. Experimental evaluation on five benchmark datasets demonstrates the superiority of our method over state-of-the-art unsupervised and weakly-supervised baselines across multiple metrics. Notably, on the HumanActivityDataset, our method achieves state-of-the-art unsupervised segmentation performance, and on other datasets, our method significantly outperforms baselines while requiring an order of magnitude less computation. The EXOPLINES project has developed a comprehensive database of absorption cross-sections for various molecular species, covering a broad range from 0.1 to 100 micrometers. This includes molecules relevant to cool H-stars, brown dwarfs, and giant exoplanatmospheres, with a focus on the L, T, and Y spectral types. To ensure accuracy, we have carefully evaluated and selected only the most reliable datasets from peer-reviewed literature. Based on a thorough analysis of error patterns, we have also developed novel corrections to refine the cross-sections and improve their consistency with benchmark values. This process has involved a detailed examination of 158 datasets, accounting for various isotopic variants and energy level discrepancies. As a result, we have established error estimates for each cross-section, with an average margin of error below 10%. To facilitate future updates, we have developed an open-source framework using the PyMieLab library, allowing for easy access to our dataset at https://github.com/astro-hydra/exoplines. This resource provides a consistent and standardized interface for using the cross-sections in atmospheric modeling, while also enabling users to request new species or energy level datasets. Furthermore, we have also identified areas for future research and data collection to support ongoing efforts to improve our understanding of cool star and giant planet atmospheres. This includes specific recommendations for 11 molecular species, 7 of which are relevant to exoplanet science. This work is expected to have a significant impact on the development of future modeling and simulation tools, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of the astrophysical environment. Traditional methods for estimating parameters of a probability distribution, such as those used for variance, skewness, and kurtosis, rely on knowledge of the underlying probability model and compute statistics like mean, unadjusted skewness, and the Fisher–Pitman kurtosis estimator. These estimates are sensitive to outliers and lack the benefits of high-breakdown point estimators like the median. A proposed solution uses the Pearson distribution to derive estimators for skewness and kurtosis that are resistant to outliers and don't require knowledge of the underlying distribution. The new estimators are compared to their counterparts for sample skewness and kurtosis by analyzing their asymptotic properties and performance through Monte Carlo simulations. The research further demonstrates that these estimators can be used to estimate location parameters like the median and scale parameters like interquartile range with improved robustness. The benefits of these improved estimators are shown in a real-world finite sample setting. The methodology is extended to handle grouped-data analysis with limited replication. The research also provides a new estimator for the scale parameter of the Cauchy distribution and offers a computational solution to the maximum depth problem. The findings suggest that highly robust estimators can be derived from distribution moments and are effective in practical scenarios. Over the past ten years, significant advancements have been made in the development of approximate query algorithms. These filters, in particular, have seen rapid progress. They operate by returning an approximate result to a query, with the aim of reducing storage needs while increasing throughput. This class of filters has been further refined into two distinct types: hamming and bipartite. Each variant excels in specific contexts - bipartite generally outperforms hamming in collections with fewer false positives, whereas hamming performs better in collections with fewer false negatives. Researchers have attempted to bridge this gap by creating hybrid filters that outperform both hamming and bipartite variants, often resulting in false positives. This paper presents a novel approach, building upon existing knowledge to create a hybrid filter with a false positive free result collection, effectively unifying previously separate aspects of this type of filtering. The proposed collection provides a versatile platform for further development and is used as a foundation to create a hybrid filter that surpasses both hamming and bipartite variants, with the lowest total storage needs across multiple evaluation datasets. This innovation also allows the creation of a lightweight filter that outperforms even lightweight filters like Topus, with the added benefit of reduced storage demands. Research in deep learning has focused on transfer learning due to its potential to reduce the need for domain-specific data. A key challenge is understanding which features are most relevant to a task, making transferability a crucial concept in deep learning. It has been observed that certain general characteristics are shared across different domains, while others are unique to each domain, influencing transfer learning. We argue that two widely-held beliefs about transferability are flawed: (1) features from the central part of a model are most relevant to a task, and (2) models with a larger scope tend to be more transferable. Through experiments using gAP, a novel attribution tool, we demonstrate that features from the tail of a model are more indicative of a task and that reducing the model's complexity can actually increase transferability, counterintuitive as it may seem. Our findings have significant implications for the design of models, encouraging the use of less complex architectures that are easier to adapt to new tasks. We have released our code to facilitate further research. 

In addition, we have conducted a series of experiments to verify our claims. Firstly, we have tested the influence of adding artificial noise to the input on the transferability of pre-trained models, observing that those with less regularisation, i.e. those with noise added to the input, tend to be more transferable. This supports our hypothesis that reducing the model's complexity can increase transferability. 

We have also investigated the transferability of features from different parts of an image, discovering that those from the edge of an image are more transferable than those from the central region. This contradicts the commonly-held belief that features from the central part of an image are more transferable. 

Finally, we have tested whether models with a larger scope are more transferable, comparing the transferability of models with a non-linear layer versus those without. Our results show that those without a non-linear layer are more transferable, contradicting the commonly-held belief that models with a larger scope are more transferable. 

In summary, our experiments have revealed that two widely-held beliefs about transferability are incorrect: features from the tail of a model are more transferable than those from the head, and reducing the model's complexity can increase transferability. 

This has significant implications for the design of models, encouraging the use of less complex architectures that are easier to adapt to new tasks. 

Our code has been released to facilitate further research. 

A novel attribution tool, gAP, has been developed to support our claims.

Recent studies have suggested that global protoplanetary disk flows and turbulence could significantly influence pebble accretion. However, the impact of associated density fluctuations remains unexplored. We find that these fluctuations can reduce pebble accretion by a planet of a certain size, providing a possible solution to the planet formation timescale issue. This could be a critical factor in the formation of massive gas giants. Researchers have been trying to understand its underlying basis, but its intuitive connection with computational constraints has not been thoroughly explored. This paper aims to highlight the significance of considering computational limitations in learning theory by demonstrating how certain problems with limited computational resources benefit from overparameterization. The study focuses on neural networks with ReLU activations and demonstrates that, within specific computational constraints, overparameterization can be essential for avoiding memorization and achieving generalization. The findings suggest that overparameterization is not only a useful tool but also, in some cases, a necessary one for tackling real-world learning challenges. Furthermore, the study emphasizes the importance of taking computational limitations into account when designing and understanding machine learning algorithms. This study addresses the urban dial-a-ride problem, which involves determining the most cost-effective way to meet the transportation needs of elderly or mobility-impaired individuals in a city. Each user requires a journey-based trip request, and a vehicle can be shared among multiple riders. We consider the practical constraints of user demands, vehicle capacities, route travel times, and parking availability, aiming to minimize total trip costs. A mixed-integer linear optimization model is developed to solve this problem, taking into account fixed costs for vehicle usage and rider trips. However, solving this model is computationally challenging due to non-linear vehicle variable costs, which can be mitigated by developing a novel branch-and-cut method. This method integrates standard path-constraint cuts, such as commodity cuts and cutgesco, as well as new parking constraint cuts. We test and evaluate our approach on a range of instances with up to 12 users and 2 vehicles, observing significant reductions in computation time. Our results also highlight the effectiveness of the novel parking constraint cut cutgeco, which can further accelerate solution times. Furthermore, our analysis explores the impact of vehicle variable costs on optimal solutions, revealing that these costs can substantially influence the feasibility of user demands. In summary, our research provides a comprehensive analysis of the urban dial-a-ride problem, along with an innovative optimization approach that is well-suited for practical applications. These devices are typically validated using controlled clinical trials that compare AI-generated results with those of human healthcare professionals against actual patient outcomes. Predicting social human motion requires a consideration of both short-term dynamics (e.g. avoiding collisions) and long-term patterns (e.g. attending a meeting). Current approaches often focus on one or the other, with little attention to how they interact. Moreover, most existing predicters can only forecast a few steps ahead, making it difficult to build more reliable and accurate long-term prediction models. To address these limitations, we present a new end-to-end probabilistic approach that uses a socially-aware representation of human intentions and interactions. By modeling the probability of a person's future trajectory as a sequence of conditional probabilities at successive time points, our new method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on public datasets. Training data is derived from a variational graph autoencoder that captures the spatial relationships between people, while our new method uses a sliding window of past states to improve its accuracy. Moreover, our new method uses a socially-aware representation of human intentions and interactions, achieving state-of-the-art results on public datasets. The proposed method can predict multiple future steps as a sequence of conditional probabilities at successive time points, demonstrating its potential as a real-time predictor. To validate our approach, we conduct a series of experiments that compare its performance to other socially-aware prediction methods. The results show that our new method outperforms other socially-aware prediction methods in terms of accuracy and reliability. Moreover, our new method achieves significant improvements in accuracy and reliability, with gains of up to 15% and 20% respectively over state-of-the-art techniques on the SUNCG dataset. This study examines the relationships among measures of complexity in a subset of Boltzmann machines, distinguishing between those that gauge internal complexity and those that account for connections between interconnected hidden and visible units. To explore these differences, we calculate various information-theoretic measures of complexity and conduct statistical analyses to determine correlations among these metrics, as well as among the complexity of individual units and the network as a whole. Furthermore, in an effort to develop more effective methods for assessing Boltzmann machines, we apply principal components analysis to the space of possible complexity values to identify dimensions where the metrics of complexity exhibit distinct behaviors. Ultimately, through our numerical investigations, we identify dimensions where the internal complexity of units appears to diverge from the complexity of units influenced by hidden units, thereby informing an understanding of the structure of Boltzmann machines and providing a foundation for the development of novel algorithms for generating complex architectures in future research. The complexity of visible units, in contrast, is found to diverge from the complexity of the network as a whole. As a result, our findings provide a starting point for the creation of more efficient methods for assessing Boltzmann machines in a broader range of settings. The present work is a preliminary investigation, and we have specifically chosen a subset of Boltzmann machines as a straightforward starting point for our study before expanding our focus to more general architectures in the future. A driving protocol called counterdiabatic is extremely efficient, transferring a quantum system from a initial state to a target state with minimal disturbance. However, creating customised driving protocols for complex many-body systems like the Hubbard model is very difficult. A new approach uses a variational method to create a counterdiabatic protocol without needing a detailed Hamiltonian description. When applied to the one-dimensional Hubbard model, the results show that this method effectively switches on the interactions in the system without inducing disturbances that exceed those caused by the harmonic generator Hamiltonian. Moreover, the approach works in higher dimensions and is applicable to a wide range of many-body systems. Notably, the approach initialises ground states effectively in half-filled systems and is resistant to time-variation. A major advantage of this approach is that it only requires a limited number of controllable Hamiltonian parameters and does not need to be highly precise. This technique has numerous applications, such as analyzing production functions in economics to measure productivity growth or identifying the optimal combination of factors necessary for production. Another useful approach, least squares multi-product approximation, can help fit complex functions involving multiple variables, often used for modeling production frontiers. Researchers have found that the LSMS algorithm achieves faster convergence and more stable results compared to traditional methods like frontier estimation using a non-parametric maximum likelihood approach. This paper presents a new open-source library, pyStoNED, designed to simplify the process of using these algorithms for their respective tasks. Finally, using a dataset on global CO2 emissions, the authors demonstrate the effectiveness of the LSMS algorithm in fitting complex functions involving multiple variables. Overall, the new toolkit makes it easier to fit production functions and other complex data sets using the latest convex regression techniques. Most kernel-based techniques rely heavily on exchangeability assumptions, 
which can be overly restrictive. To broaden the scope of these techniques, 
we suggest a new class of kernels called Non-Exchangeable Tangent Kernels 
(NFT-K), that can capture more nuanced characteristics of highly structured 
data sets. NFT-K kernels combine exchangeable kernels with data index functions 
that incorporate external information, like image labels or geolocation. 
By leveraging this extra information, NFT-K can recognize and exploit patterns 
within highly structured data sets more effectively. In our study, NFT-K outperforms 
exchangeable kernels on a range of complex tasks, including graph classification 
and geolocation-based image analysis. NFT-K is highly adaptable and can be easily 
integrated into a variety of learning pipelines and techniques. We provide theoretical 
justification for NFT-K's effectiveness and demonstrate its potential applications. 
Furthermore, NFT-K provides a framework for incorporating prior knowledge into 
learning models, allowing for more informed data analysis. As a result, NFT-K 
offers a significant advancement in the field of kernel-based learning. We make NFT-K 
publicly available at https://github.com/nygath/nft-k. 

Please note that this work was originally published in 2021. Any related publications 
may have been delayed due to COVID-19 related timing discrepancies.

  into learning models.

The protection mechanism provided by time-reversal symmetry in non-Hermitian topological systems is susceptible to disruption from correlations. This implies that even in systems where local interactions are weak, correlations can still induce gap closing. Notably, a comprehensive classification of corrosion-induced gap closing is not yet established, and we identify a novel category of such an event, which we refer to as the correlation-induced fractional topological phase (CIFTP). The CIFTP is characterized by its fractional nature and the closing gap's involvement with high-energy states. In various fields, researchers examine how self-organizing systems, governed by stochastic dynamics, can develop and sustain patterns over time. A key aspect of these systems is the emergence of features that can be passed on from one generation to the next, which fundamentally alters the system's trajectory. We urge the community to recognize that such heritable information is an integral component of these systems, and its presence or absence should be explicitly stated when investigating their underlying stochastic evolution. In our study, we illustrate this concept through two examples: one involving a system driven by mutation and limited replication, and another with a system governed by energy input and thermal equilibrium. By modeling these systems as sequences of patterns evolving over time, we establish a mathematical framework for understanding their patterns and analyze their potential for heritable information. In the first system, our results confirm that only those with a limited number of replicative capacity are capable of sustaining and passing on patterns, and that this number can be quantified. In the case of systems in thermal equilibrium, our analysis reveals that only a small subset of possible configurations is suitable for heritable information, and that this subset is typically extremely difficult to access. By integrating our findings with the broader context of self-organizing systems, we explore the implications of our research and suggest that the system governed by the Wigner random matrix ensemble may be an example of a system unable to sustain heritable information over time. Ultimately, our study seeks to inspire a deeper understanding of the interplay between stochastic dynamics, heritable information, and the emergence of patterns in self-organizing systems. A major global issue persists, characterized by the presence of intestinal parasites in the human gastrointestinal system, often transmitted through contaminated food, water, and direct contact.  These parasites cause a range of severe health problems, including chronic diseases, inflammation, and life-threatening conditions.  Traditional methods of identifying these parasites rely heavily on manual examination, a labor-intensive and costly process.  This research aims to develop an efficient computer-aided system for categorizing intestinal parasites.  A dataset of 1,600 images, each depicting one of four distinct species (Ascaris lumbricoides, Hymenolepis nana, Opisthorchis viverrini, and Toxocara cati), was compiled and optimized for the task.  A Deep Belief Network model, trained on images resized to 227x227, achieved a 70% accuracy score.  Furthermore, the paper proposes an image preprocessing pipeline, designed to improve the accuracy of parasite species identification processes.  This method involves the detection and removal of background noise through histogram manipulation and image sharpening using the unsharp masking technique.  The results demonstrate that the combination of this preprocessing method and the DBN model achieves superior results compared to traditional background removal techniques.  The proposed system is expected to serve as a valuable tool for medical professionals, aiding in the diagnosis and treatment of intestinal parasite-related diseases.  A potential extension of the research could involve the integration of this system with a medical database, providing a comprehensive diagnostic tool for healthcare providers. The estimation of temperature anisotropies in the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) through maximum likelihood methods often involves a trade-off between achieving high signal-to-noise ratios and minimizing uncertainties related to instrumental noise and foreground emissions. This trade-off is particularly challenging when addressing point sources that, due to their localized nature, require precise localization techniques for accurate estimation. This, in turn, demands a larger number of parameters than typically desired for maximum likelihood estimation. To circumvent this issue, we explore an alternative approach that combines an initial, likelihood-based estimation of diffuse foregrounds and point sources with a subsequent, separate estimation of instrumental noise using a minimum description length criterion. This method, which employs an "outside-in" strategy, can significantly alleviate the tension between signal strength and estimation uncertainty. Numerical simulations using real-world data from the LAMBDA2 and Planck surveys demonstrate the effectiveness of this solution in enhancing the overall performance of CMB maps in terms of both signal detection and parameter estimation accuracy. Furthermore, our proposed method has been successfully applied to the recent BICEP/Keck data release, yielding reliable CMB map estimates free from point source contamination artifacts. This method represents a significant advancement, enabling the creation of robust, reliable CMB maps even in the presence of point sources. As such, it holds considerable potential for a wide range of applications, including the estimation of polarization data, cross-spectrum analysis, and cosmological parameter estimation. Ultimately, the adoption of this technique may facilitate the removal of x-marking artifacts in recent CMB data releases, such as the BICEP/Keck 2019 data set. The accompanying software package, cmb_forecasts, has been developed to facilitate the reproduction of our research findings. This package provides a flexible, open-source codebase enabling the generation of realistic CMB data sets, model simulations, and associated forecasts, while also supporting the "outside-in" estimation approach described above. Furthermore, the method is shown to improve robustness against latent variable perturbations, making it a desirable technique for critical systems. [Publication: ICML 2020]

This paper presents an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on
successful autoencoding techniques, yielding high quality speech using only
unlabeled audio and text data. Diverging from complex, highly parameterized
models, we propose a straightforward, autoencoding architecture with a mere
6,332 parameters, thereby facilitating both training and speech synthesis tasks
to be readily performed on typical GPUs. Furthermore, our model exhibits a
notable ability to generalize beyond seen contexts, with capacity limits being
discussed through experimentation. Evaluation results demonstrate the superiority
of our model over a baseline, as well as over an open-source, commercially
developed unsupervised speech synthesis system. All training procedures were
performed on a single GPU, producing synthesis examples at approximately 1.5
hours per epoch. As an added benefit, our model's simplicity also enables direct
visual inspection of the learned latent space, providing valuable insights into
the relationship between acoustic features and linguistic context. This research is
the first to achieve state-of-the-art performance on speech synthesis without
supervised training. A software implementation of this work is available at

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world contexts, notably in mechanical engineering. This research presents a novel algorithm, combining a multi-criteria branch-and-bound technique with non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm- II. Diverging from traditional multi-criteria branch-and-bound methods, our approach employs non-dominated sorting to create initial populations and eliminate inferior branches. Additionally, it leverages elite solutions found along the way to fill in the Pareto front gaps encountered. This algorithm is then evaluated using two test cases: the multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear optimization problem based on the well-known cantilever design problem and a multi-objective formulation of the strength optimization design problem under multiple load scenarios. Our results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm produces accurate Pareto front results for small to medium-sized complex MO-MINLPs. Moreover, our findings indicate that it outperforms NSGA-II, yielding more precise solutions with fewer function evaluations. This superior performance is attributed to the efficient non-dominated sorting-based population screening mechanism, which greatly reduces computational costs. This technique has the potential to enhance the speed of multi-criteria branch-and-bound algorithms. The way people express emotions varies greatly, with some expressing their feelings openly and directly, while others may not even realize they're expressing their emotions. To capture this emotional nuance, we need more sophisticated emotion representation models that can learn emotions from both explicit and implicit patterns of expression. To address this need, we developed a new approach to emotion representation that involves a two-part training process. Firstly, we train a model to recognize when two pieces of text share similar emotional patterns, and secondly, we train the model to contrast the differences between an explicit label and the implicit text emotions. This approach enables our model to learn emotions in a variety of contexts and improves its overall performance by up to 11% compared to state-of-the-art methods on the latest datasets for sentiment analysis that requires aspect-based analysis. We publicly share our code with these findings to facilitate future research. We also conducted an additional set of experiments to examine how our approach performs in cross-domain settings and found that it can handle this challenge effectively, even when the emotional patterns differ significantly. This paper presents a new multilingual dataset, MEE, containing over 6,000 English and 1,000 French event descriptions gathered from news sources. Each event in MEE has been annotated to include relevant spatial, temporal, and causal details. This dataset allows models to demonstrate their ability to process causal information, making decisions about multiple languages possible. Initial experiments conducted on MEE reveal that using pre-trained T5 models and masked language modeling leads to high performance levels, with over 90% accuracy in English and 85% in French. However, further studies indicate that several significant biases affect the MEE dataset, influencing model performance during evaluation. Potential applications and future research directions for MEE are also explored. The dataset, accompanied by accompanying code and models, can be accessed at a designated repository. This work further examines the challenges associated with French processing in NLP by highlighting 20 key issues and proposing potential solutions. Finally, a comprehensive evaluation of MEE's impact on related NLP tasks is presented.

Recent studies have examined how language models represent and process textual information, but similar investigations for models integrating visual and language inputs are scarce. Our work involves modifying the GPT3 model to incorporate a visual processing capability, represented as O, which enables it to remember and use visual data to inform text generation in subsequent outputs. Our studies indicate that incorporating GPT3-O can lead to text generation improvements in coherence and engagement metrics in various scenarios, including human-written short stories and knowledge-based articles. Notably, we found that including the visual aspect didn't necessarily result in more factual accuracy, and including GPT-O interactions did not enhance our results. Our results suggest that incorporating visual processing into language models like GPT3 is possible and can lead to text generation improvements. The code and models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/gpt-o. Our results also raise important ethical considerations, highlighted in the pre-print's discussion section, which warrant further attention. The GPT3-O modifications were enabled by utilizing the language model interface of Facebook's LAMPS framework. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT protocol builds upon the existing RingCT protocol used in the Bytecoin blockchain, integrating it with DPoS for the first time.
The implementation of DPoS in the Bytecoin blockchain enhances transaction finality and user experience, making it more comparable to other public blockchains.
The Delegated RingCT protocol on the Bytecoin blockchain achieves greater privacy benefits than other DPoS-based blockchains, such as Bitcoin Forks or other privacy-focused blockchains that lack transaction finality.
The Delegated RingCT protocol on Bytecoin enables approximately double the number of ring signatures compared to its non-delegated counterpart, RingCT, while maintaining a constant size limit for transaction encoding.
In addition, Delegated RingCT also enables greater flexibility in transaction creation through the introduction of a new compact mode, allowing non-specialized users to generate transactions more easily.
The performance of the Delegated RingCT protocol on Bytecoin demonstrates its potential for significant improvements in transaction finality and user experience.
The open-source code for Delegated RingCT is available for immediate use, enabling developers to implement this solution on other blockchain platforms. 
In particular, Delegated RingCT could potentially be integrated with Zcash as a more efficient and flexible alternative to Zk-Snarks, achieving improved results compared to its non-delegated counterpart, Zcash. 
The results of Delegated RingCT on Bytecoin demonstrate its viability as a scalable and efficient privacy solution for DPoS-based blockchains. 
The integration of DPoS and Ring signatures achieves a breakthrough in transaction finality and user experience, making Delegated RingCT a promising solution for blockchains seeking to balance privacy and usability with transaction finality. 
Ultimately, Delegated RingCT has the potential to be a versatile solution for a wide range of blockchain platforms. 
In the future, researchers can conduct thorough security assessments of Delegated RingCT to identify potential areas of improvement and mitigate security risks. 
The results of these security assessments can inform future research and development on Delegated RingCT and other privacy solutions for blockchains. 
In addition, future research can explore the integration of Delegated RingCT with other cutting-edge blockchain technologies, such as sharding and Proof of Stake Voting, to further enhance its scalability and usability. 
The results of this research can inform the development of more efficient and effective privacy solutions

The study relies on a helicity model to determine the angular distributions of the decay products. We propose a novel optimization technique, specifically designed for training quantized neural networks. This method, called AskewSGD, can be integrated into existing stochastic gradient descent algorithms to efficiently converge towards the optimal model for quantized neural networks. AskewSGD overcomes underconfidence (being too confident in predictions) and overconfidence issues by dynamically adjusting learning rates and applying regularization. This is achieved by perturbing weights within a restricted interval during backward propagation, an approach inspired by existing methods. In addition, we provide theoretical justifications for the optimization technique, validating its convergence and establishing the optimal convergence rate. Experimental results demonstrate that AskewSGD outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches, leading to significant improvements in accuracy, with a notable increase of up to 1.5% when using 4-bit quantization on CIFAR10, while also reducing training time by a factor of 2.5x. AskewSGD's efficiency enables post-training quantization deployments to be executed 1.5x faster. This method can also be applied to existing libraries such as PyTorch with minimal modifications, facilitating deployment. AskewSGD's source code can be accessed on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/andrebarba/AskewSGD. In addition, we provide pre-trained quantized models for common datasets on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/andrebarba/AskewSGD-pre-trained-models. The task of fact verification involves confirming the accuracy of specific claims, 
such as "Tom Cruise won an Oscar." To accomplish this, systems must be able to identify 
relevant information, like awards won by an actor, and also recognize what the 
statement is attempting to disprove - in this instance, that an Oscar was not received. 
Current methods rely on pre-existing knowledge databases, but often fail to account for 
essential details, such as how the statement can be broken down into its constituent 
parts, and specific steps are required to confirm the claim. To address these limitations, 
a new approach called DisVBERT has been developed. It utilizes disassembly analysis to 
break down statements into their fundamental components and identifies the specific 
aspects that the claim seeks to confirm or deny. By applying this technique, the model 
achieves superior performance on the FACTCHECKNET dataset, outperforming the best 
previous models significantly. Moreover, experiments confirm that disassembly-based 
disintegration contributes substantially to the model's overall performance. To facilitate 
further exploration of this new method, the source code and pre-trained models for 
DisVBERT have been made publicly available. Evaluation results and model parameters 
can also be found in the accompanying repository. Research has been supported by a 
grant from the National Science Foundation. Models were trained on an AMD Ryzen 9 
5800X processor and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 GPU, and the majority of experiments 
involved data processing on an AMD EPYC 7742 server. Additionally, the research was 
conducted in a controlled environment with a stable network connection provided by 
a Netgear Nighthawk AX6 router. To facilitate model training, the model was 
initially fine-tuned on the Enron-BNC corpus using a 256GB Samsung SSD 970 EVO 
solid-state drive. DisVBERT models were then saved to a 1TB external hard drive for 
archival purposes. To support the research, the model was initially reviewed by Dr. 
Chenhuan Liu, and later discussed with Dr. Weiliang Chen. To enable reproducibility, 
the model training and testing source code and models have been made publicly available 
on the GitHub platform.

We've developed a novel variant of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) called Hidden Space Conditioning (HSC), which introduces robust control over latent variable dynamics within a specific cluster using normalizing flows, while preserving cluster boundaries. HSC outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in density estimation for multi-modal data distributions, particularly in generating high-quality samples in 3DMesh, MNIST, and Frechet Fashion, according to the Frechet distance metric. Furthermore, our approach surpasses Fixed Latent Space (FLS) and other established methods in learning multi-modal data representations and Frechet distances in tasks involving classification on structured data, such as Point Clouds and 3DMesh. Notably, our technique demonstrates improved performance in generating semi-realistic Point Clouds when conditioning on partial shapes, a challenging problem. Our code is available at https://github.com/andreabp/hsc.

A widely employed technique called Nested Sampling combines a random sampling approach with a non-linear estimation method to model complex probability distributions. The success of this algorithm heavily relies on a suitable step selection function, which identifies eligible candidates to remove from the sample pool. This paper examines and compares various step selectors that support Nested Sampling, including the original Nestle implementation's default method, a maximum likelihood-based approach, a Bayesian shrinkage technique, a machine learning-based algorithm, and a novel information-theoretic strategy. The chosen step selectors are integrated into the widely used Dulpy implementation of Nested Sampling. The proposed methods are thoroughly tested using Dulpy's Bayesian workflow on diverse Bayesian models and datasets. The experimental results indicate that the newly introduced step selectors generally surpass the existing ones in performance, with the information-theoretic approach emerging as the superior option. The associated code is openly accessible via https://github.com/andreberg/nested-sampling. The findings of this study are expected to benefit the development of future Nested Sampling algorithms. The Dulpy integration of these new step selectors is intended to improve the analysis of complex probability distributions in real-world applications. The open-source nature of this work aims to stimulate further advancements in Nested Sampling algorithm development. Analysis of the results suggests that the performance of the information-theoretic approach can be further optimized by only removing the sample with the lowest likelihood within each slice, with the associated code made available on GitHub. This revised implementation is expected to result in better performance, with the open-source nature of this work aimed at stimulating future advancements in Nested Sampling algorithm development. The implementation is available on GitHub at https://github.com/andreberg/nested-sampling. A subsequent study has built upon these findings, incorporating the established results into the widely used Dulpy implementation of Nested Sampling. The associated Dulpy integration is available on GitHub at https://github.com/andreberg/dulpy. In various fields, there is a growing need for efficient algorithms that create and utilize distance labellings with an increased tolerance for errors. As such, we propose an algorithm that assigns unique labels to the vertices of a planar graph to facilitate distance computation with an allowable margin for measurement inaccuracies. Our proposed approach builds upon an existing distance labelling method and enhances it with an error-correcting mechanism inspired by fault-tolerant spanning tree design. Our algorithm accommodates any given distance labelling method, but it is particularly tailored to those that utilise omnidirectional monodirectional labellings. Furthermore, we provide evidence that demonstrating the optimality of traditional distance labellings does not necessarily imply the optimality of fault-resilient variants, but we do offer a generalised solution that applies to all omnidirectional labellings. Our algorithm performs well in practical scenarios, but its theoretical efficiency is a factor of O(n^2) with respect to input vertices. Nevertheless, we do offer a more efficient variant that achieves a time and space complexity of O(n log n) for specific types of planar graphs known as trapezoid graphs. Our algorithm's correctness and performance are supported by experimental results, which demonstrate its superiority to traditional distance labellings in error-prone environments. Our investigation into the performance of fault-resilient labellings on a range of test cases reveals that our proposed approach outperforms a more conservative method that assigns redundant labels to ensure error correction. Our results confirm the existence of significant benefits to using fault-resilient labellings in scenarios where hardware failures are a concern. Quantum fluctuations between two spatially linked qubits are explored in a Bose-Hubbard model subject to dissipation and forced two-body interactions. The impact of dissipation is initially found to weaken the maximum anti-correlation signal when the qubits are in proximity, yet subsequent forced coupling causes a resurgence of this anti-correlation signal. The resulting time-domain two-qubit correlation functions display intricate, non-monotonic patterns in both the driving amplitude and duration. Furthermore, frequency-domain analysis via quantum cospectral mapping reveals the emergence of an extended autoionization process affecting the highest autoionization line when the qubits are close, while an autoionization doublet is observed for the lower lines. The study demonstrates that time-domain two-qubit correlations can be manipulated by adjusting the system's parameters. Moreover, an extended autoionization process of highly entangled states can be achieved through an extended autoionization line shape. The research was carried out using a custom-made quantum simulator based on Python's QuTiP library. The study's findings are expected to contribute to the understanding of quantum fluctuations in complex quantum systems. The associated code can be found at the GitHub repository: https://github.com/Chen-Bo-Qing/Quantum_fluctuations_in_coupled_qubits.

Out-of-distribution (OoD) detection has become a crucial task in the field of machine learning. It involves identifying scenarios where a model is asked a question outside its previously learned domain. Our research focuses on developing an OoD detection method that leverages the uncertainty information inherent in Bayesian deep learning. By applying a distributional approximation to Gaussian Process-based deep learning methods, we derive an analytical expression for the predictive process, enabling the identification of OoD cases based on the predictive distribution's properties. Our proposed approach is validated by comparing it to existing baselines on both simulated and real-world datasets in image classification tasks. Moreover, we demonstrate its effectiveness in integrating uncertainty information from the predictive shift to enhance OoD detection performance. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/andreabibbo/dgp-ood. According to our results, the proposed method outperforms or matches the performance of state-of-the-art OoD detection methods in most cases. Notably, the results on CIFAR10-R and CIFAR100-R datasets show that DGP-based approaches are less sensitive to noise compared to other baselines. Overall, the research highlights the potential of distributional approximations in Gaussian Process-based deep learning to effectively address OoD detection challenges. Our analysis also suggests that further research is necessary to explore the relationship between predictive uncertainty and OoD detection, potentially leading to the development of more robust OoD detection methods. We investigate adaptive decision-making in situations involving delays that depend on specific conditions, which can either be known beforehand or unpredictable. In the context of advice-seeking, an observer seeks an optimal strategy for executing a series of tasks based on recommendations from an advisor, while taking into account varying execution times that are contingent upon the tasks themselves and may be characterized by an advisor. When execution times are influenced by specific circumstances and not just their sequence (delay-minimal setting), or when they are unpredictable and only the observer has access to their distribution (non-stochastic setting, or delay-adaptive environment)) quite a few fundamental problems of bandits remain unsolved. This paper presents the first algorithms capable of addressing these challenges. When execution times are influenced by specific circumstances and not just their sequence (delay-minimal setting), we developed an adaptive algorithm that ensures a cumulative reward of at least $\Omega\left(\sqrt{2T \log N} \right)$ over $T$ rounds, which is within $O(\log \log T)$ of the optimal reward in the worst case. When execution times are unpredictable and only the observer has access to their distribution (delay-adaptive environment), we developed an adaptive algorithm that ensures a cumulative reward of at least $\frac{1}{2} \log T + \log \log T + \log \log \log T$ for $T$ rounds, which is close to the optimal reward in the worst case. These results are obtained by assuming that the observer receives recommendations from an advisor who is unable to affect the outcome of the tasks themselves. This paper also presents a new non-adaptive algorithm for the case in which execution times are influenced by specific circumstances and not just their sequence (delay-minimal setting), which ensures a cumulative reward of at least $\Omega\left(\sqrt{T \log N} \right)$. This algorithm is based on a new construction of a $t$-design in the space of execution times, which is the first to be proposed in the literature. It is worth noting that the non-adaptive algorithm for the case in which execution times are influenced by specific circumstances and not just their sequence (delay-minimal setting)) has been proven to be optimal to the best of our knowledge. Although these methods can be highly effective, they are hindered by two significant drawbacks. Firstly, they struggle to produce text that accurately reflects the nuances of human language, particularly in terms of its complexity. Secondly, they require either an abundance of available data or an extensive number of interactions, which can be difficult to facilitate in many practical applications.

VACA utilizes a latent representation that captures node-specific class probabilities both with and without the influence of specific interventions, all within a single integrated framework. We demonstrate that VACA can be implemented by combining two separate variational autoencoder models, which must only agree on their latent representations. We also prove that VACA's representations meet key requirements for causal reasoning tasks. Our experiments with both synthetic and real-world data show that VACA effectively generates causal knowledge representations, leading to several state-of-the-art causal deep learning models that can utilize these representations to make accurate predictions.
