The emergence of pre-trained multilingual language models has significantly accelerated the development of advanced information retrieval models.  Utilizing these models, cross lingual information retrieval (CLIR) can now directly use multilingual text for retrieval instead of traditional approaches which used query translation.  CLIR can now be treated as a single CLM (cross lingual matching) task.  However existing CLM models are not fully utilizing the potential of multilingual text as they are trained in two separate modes - interactive where multiple sentences are considered in relation to the query and non-interactive where only single sentences related to the query are considered.  In this study we propose a new framework called ViNIR, that combines the benefits of both interactive and non-interactive models for CLIR.  It does so by first extracting a relevant context from the multilingual text and then using a query to select a relevant context and finally use a learned cross lingual matching function to rank the contexts.  This context ranking can then be used to retrieve relevant documents.  In order to achieve this, ViNIR leverages interactive models to extract context and non-interactive models for cross lingual document ranking.  In order to prevent overfitting, a simple yet effective early stopping criterion is used.  We test the framework on different datasets and evaluate it using different retrieval metrics and find that it significantly outperforms state of the art techniques.  Moreover, a human evaluation is also conducted and the results from both retrieval metrics and human evaluation confirm the superiority of ViNIR over existing state of the art techniques.  This study is the first to explore the benefits of interactive and non-interactive models for CLIR and it opens up new avenues of research in this area.  It also sets a new benchmark for CLIR models and it can potentially revolutionize the field of CLIR.  This study is available at https://github.com/thesaipal/vinir.  In addition to that, a new dataset called multlingual wikipedia which is required for training and testing ViNIR is also made available at https://github.com/thesaipal/vinir-data.  This dataset can also be used to test and evaluate the performance of existing state of the art techniques. Object Detection, a core Computer Vision task, has seen significant advancements
in recent years, but current models still face challenges when it comes to
identifying object categories beyond those seen during the model's training phase.
This limitation is due in part to the high cost associated with manually annotating
objects. A major issue with current semi-supervised learning techniques is that
they generate incomplete and imprecise object bounding-box labels for unseen
categories, which hinders their performance. To address this problem, we propose
a new method that generates high-quality bounding-box labels for any given image
and category combination through a combination of image segmentation and category
recognition. Our method then employs these generated labels in an iterative
semi-supervised learning framework to improve the model's performance on seen and
unseen categories. This approach outperforms state-of-the-art models while
requiring only basic hardware to train. Our experiments demonstrate that the
model can recognize over 1,000 categories with just 10,000 manually annotated
labels, which is a significant reduction in required annotations of nearly two

The integrity of the information society relies heavily on the credibility of the data it produces. As the amount of online content grows, so do concerns about its reliability, leading to a significant amount of misinformation circulating on social media, which can lead to severe consequences. Despite efforts to address this problem by various platforms, the issue persists. In contrast, fact-checking initiatives have achieved some success, albeit with limitations due to scalability and cost constraints. To improve the efficiency and effectiveness of misinformation detection, recent advancements in natural language generation and machine learning have focused on utilizing transformer models. This paper provides an in-depth review of the recent applications and achievements of transformer-based models in misinformation identification, with an emphasis on the significance of semantic representation in this context. It also explores the advantages of using transformer models, such as capturing complex contextual dependencies, and highlights their potential limitations, including requiring substantial computational resources. Additionally, the survey delves into the various types of misinformation, such as deepfakes and disinformation, and the methods employed to detect them, including neural networks and the use of additional data sources. Furthermore, the paper discusses the importance of contextual information in the field and offers recommendations for future advancements, such as integrating third-party verification services and the potential risks of relying on user-generated data. Ultimately, the survey concludes by suggesting future research directions and potential applications of transformer-based models for detecting various types of misinformation. With the rapid advancement of misinformation, the survey aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the subject matter, essential for addressing this critical issue. Misinformation is a pressing global problem that demands immediate attention, and this paper strives to contribute to the ongoing discussions by shedding light on the latest developments in this field. Although the survey is not exhaustive, it covers a substantial amount of ground, and future researchers can build upon this foundation to take the discussion further. This paper investigates the underlying causes of interference in neural architecture search (NAS), a novel challenge distinct from interference seen in language models. It reveals that interference in NAS manifests as a cathodic effect where samples influence the architecture of other samples within the same batch, differing from the anodic effect observed in language models. To address this issue, the paper proposes an innovative method by transforming the output of each sample in a batch using a specific transformation that eliminates batch-level correlations, thereby reducing cathodic interference. Additionally, the paper introduces a controller that employs ensemble learning to combat interference and demonstrates through comprehensive evaluations that the proposed method yields superior results on complex architecture search tasks. Notably, the proposed method enables tabnet to achieve a median ensemble accuracy of 84.7% on tabular data, outperforming the state-of-the-art model with a 2% improvement. Furthermore, the proposed method enables CNAS to attain an accuracy of 84.4% on CIFAR, surpassing the state-of-the-art model with a 1% improvement. Lastly, the proposed method enables CNAS to attain an accuracy of 88.7% on CNAS challenge, outperforming the state-of-the-art model with a 1% improvement. In multitasking allocation problems, a central controller assigns tasks to agents seeking optimal task routes with minimal travel costs. Since agents may not possess all necessary skills, tasks often require assignment to suitable agents, posing a challenge. Previous research assumed each agent can handle only one task at a time, whereas we investigate an alternative setting where agents can handle multiple tasks concurrently. This variation presents unique difficulties, such as determining which tasks can be combined and which agents can handle them, as well as negotiating among agents who can solve multiple tasks simultaneously. A new class of problems, called Multitasking Allocation with Shared Processing (MASP), addresses these concerns. A solution approach for MASP is developed, comprising two optimization problems that can be solved using linear programming, alongside a new dataset and benchmark results. Additionally, we demonstrate that MASP is NP-complete and explore its relationship with a well-known problem, showing that MASP is a more challenging variant of Multi-Task Assignment (MTA). A comprehensive analysis of MASP and MTA is conducted, highlighting key differences and similarities. Experimental results demonstrate that MASP is a more complex problem than MTA, but solving it often yields solutions for MTA that outperform those found through standard methods. As a result, our solution approach for MASP can be used as a new method for resolving MTA instances. Furthermore, we propose a series of practical applications for MASP, showcasing its value in real-world scenarios. A publicly available repository containing our solution approach and benchmark results can be found at https://github.com/andrewmroberts/MASP. A companion video illustrating our approach can be found at https://youtu.be/6hjzrjw6xwA. A presentation based on this work was delivered at ICAPS 2022. A related article was published in AAAI 2021, titled Multitasking Allocation Revisited. Although it presents a different variation of the problem, the MASP approach developed here is general and can be used to find high-quality solutions for a variety of problem instances. This study investigates how a single-support hopping legged robot's movement is affected by a deformable terrain. To simulate these dynamics, a multi-body model was developed, which accounted for both the robot's leg and body and the effects of ground deformation. To estimate the effects of terrain deformation more accurately, a finite element model of the terrain was integrated with the multi-body model. Based on these models, a control strategy was designed to maximize the robot's vertical hopping velocity. When compared to a non-deformable terrain simulation, the deformable terrain simulation resulted in a significant increase in the robot's vertical velocity and stability, with some occasional benefits to horizontal velocity due to energy rebound. However, the benefit to horizontal velocity was found to be highly dependent on the terrain stiffness. While an open-loop control strategy was found to be effective, a more robust control strategy that utilizes feedback from sensors could further improve the robot's performance, with potential for even greater gains. Future work will focus on developing a feedback control strategy to enhance the robot's movement. Overall, the research demonstrates that ground deformation can have a major impact on single-support hopping robots, with potential for energy conservation through ground-robot interactions. This research could potentially be applied to other single-support robots as well. The research's findings and associated code have been shared publicly to facilitate replication and expansion upon. The research's results show that single-support hopping robots can benefit from ground deformation, which opens up new avenues for ground-up manipulation strategies. Assuming the domain, $\Omega$, has smooth boundary and its first eigenvalue satisfies $\lambda_1(\Omega) < \pi^2$, we establish an upper bound for its second Steklov eigenvalue.  Specifically, we demonstrate that $$\lambda_2(\Omega) \le 2\pi^2 + C\varepsilon^{-2}(\log(1/\varepsilon))^{-1},$$ where $C$ is a constant determined solely by the isoperimetric deficit of $\Omega$ and $\varepsilon$ represents the deviation of $\Omega$ from roundness, defined as the absolute difference between its first eigenvalue and $\pi^2$.  Furthermore, using inverse spectral geometry, we show that this estimate holds for all nearly round domains, regardless of their geometric characteristics.  Our analysis also yields an analogous estimate for the $k$th Steklov eigenvalue. Where $C_0$ is the constant from Braess and Sokolowski's work and $C$ is the constant from our work, which is dependent solely on the isoperimetric deficit of $\Omega$ and a universal bound for Steklov eigenvalues. The integration of renewable energy resources (RERs) poses significant challenges to power system expansion planning. Unchecked, these issues might lead to power system instability and obsolescence. To analyze these problems, advanced models have been developed which analyze interactions between power systems and RER integration, utilizing advanced optimization and simulation techniques. By leveraging these models, researchers can evaluate the feasibility of large-scale RER integration and propose strategies to mitigate associated complexities. However, the effectiveness of these models in power system expansion and their robustness against various scenarios have not been thoroughly studied yet. To address this gap, a study has been conducted to develop a comprehensive assessment framework for evaluating the performance of these models. This framework has been applied to five models, well-known for power system expansion, with results indicating that each model excels in specific scenarios but struggles with others. For instance, the ReEDS model performs well in coastal regions with high onshore wind resources but underperforms in landlocked areas with limited resources. Similarly, the PSAT model excels in small-scale simulations but struggles with large-scale systems. This study aims to provide a benchmark for model evaluation and shed light on the importance of model selection in power system expansion studies. It also opens the door for a more detailed comparison of these models and their applications in future research. One potential area of comparison could be model robustness, a concept that measures a model's ability to handle various scenarios and results comparable to those obtained in real-world settings. A study has been conducted to assess the robustness of these models, with results indicating that none of them can consistently perform well in all scenarios. However, certain models, such as the ReEDS and PyPSA, demonstrate relatively higher robustness compared to others. This study also identifies key factors that influence model performance and provides recommendations for model selection based on specific power system expansion applications. Finally, the study concludes with suggestions for model development, a need that has been identified in the field. By combining the findings of this study, future researchers can design and develop more effective power system expansion models, ultimately contributing to a more sustainable and resilient energy system. The comprehensive analysis and results presented in this study can serve as a valuable resource for researchers working to develop and compare power system expansion models. The corresponding code and data have been made publicly available to facilitate reproducibility and further research in this field. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/keskisalihoglu/power_system_models, while the data can be found at https://doi.org/

We establish the global existence of classical solutions for a Vlasov-Poisson-type system in a bounded area, under certain conditions on the electric potential. Furthermore, when the potential conforms to certain specifications, we demonstrate the uniqueness of these solutions. Moreover, the results are expanded to a model involving multiple particle species interacting through a specific mechanism. An important condition for these findings involves the requirement that, at a certain level, the total charge remains controlled and does not increase excessively. This research is related to models of plasmas, semiconductor devices, and dusty gases, offering theoretical support for the dynamics of these systems. An additional outcome shows that, even in the presence of a singular initial electric field, the associated electric field component in the Vlasov-Poisson model remains within certain bounds. Software maintenance tasks are often triggered by maintenance demands that require developers to locate relevant code sections based on given requirements. Research has shown that search keyword identification for code location plays a crucial role in reducing the time and effort required for software maintenance. Unfortunately, determining the relevant keywords from a given requirement is a challenging task that we aim to tackle in this paper. A new approach called STRICT has been developed to automatically extract and link keywords from a given requirement to relevant code sections in their source code. Specifically, STRICT utilizes an undirected graph model to represent a requirement, where concepts and their relationships are derived from a dictionary, and points are connected based on their shared attributes and context. A retrieval based search has been integrated into STRICT to determine the most relevant code sections. A comprehensive evaluation of STRICT was conducted using 1,515 requirements and 1,515 corresponding code sections from 30 subjects. Results showed that STRICT outperformed related techniques by accurately identifying 71% of all code sections and 51% of all keywords across all evaluations. Additionally, a post-hoc analysis highlighted the significant impact of concept-attribute density and code word density on STRICT's performance, and suggested that data-driven techniques can further improve the approach's effectiveness. The Collatz Conjecture remains an unsolved problem in the field of number theory, proposing a hypothesis that is widely regarded as one of the most enduring and intriguing unsolved problems in all of mathematics. The conjecture is based on a simple two-step process starting with any positive integer. If the number is even, it is divided by two; if it's odd, it's multiplied by three and one is added to the result. The conjecture suggests that regardless of the initial value, the sequence will eventually reach one. While many people have attempted to solve this problem, it remains unsolved, with the exception of verifying that the sequence will reach one for all numbers up to at least 20, and presenting some patterns that could potentially shed light on a possible solution. This article aims to provide an overview of the history and current developments surrounding the Collatz Conjecture. Interestingly, the conjecture is not only relevant to mathematics, as it has connections to computer science and physics as well. The article will also touch on some of the obstacles that researchers have encountered in their efforts to prove the conjecture. The author will also present some of the most recent developments and current areas of focus, highlighting the role of self-similarity, fast transients, and bias in the numbers involved. To effectively organize digital libraries and facilitate document retrieval, accurate classification is essential. In various fields, including science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM), numerous documents are published, necessitating classification. This study targets the unique challenge of classifying unseen multi-genre documents without explicit labels in a STEM context by leveraging text embeddings derived from document content. Our approach enhances classification performance by applying a two-stage process, initially incorporating a coarse taxonomy classification followed by finer-grained categorization within more defined sub-domains. Additionally, we introduce a novel task of transferring taxonomic labels across document collections, which involves transferring labels from a source set to a target set without access to the target set's annotations. This task allows us to enhance classification performance in the target set by first training on the source set. Our experiments involve multiple coarse and fine-grained taxonomies across various fields, including a significant one comprising significant volumes of unclassified documents, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. Furthermore, we evaluate the contribution of our approach against several strong baselines that perform significantly better than the state-of-the-art without any additional enhancements. Our results indicate that state-of-the-art performance can be surpassed by applying text embeddings that incorporate mathematical entity recognition. Moreover, our approach outperforms multiple strong multi-task learning and transfer learning baselines that were previously thought to be strong competitors. This research was conducted as part of a larger project, TaggerTransformer: A Multilingual and Multitask Dataset for Math and Code Recognition that was introduced in a different study. The classical stable matching problem has been extensively studied over the past 60 years with numerous applications across various disciplines. In the traditional model, where an individual can only make one proposal at a time, research has focused on key questions including "How many proposals does an individual need to make to find a stable match?" and "What is the optimal strategy for making proposals?" This paper explores a more realistic scenario where an individual can make multiple proposals simultaneously. However, in this environment, determining which proposals to make poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, we propose a concept known as "matching safety" to measure the risk of an individual's proposal being suboptimal. Our analysis reveals that while calculating this safety in an exact manner is computationally complex, we can utilize a more efficient method based on the bipartite graph matching problem to yield a practically effective solution. Furthermore, we establish that this approach is either the best or near-best method for this task. To showcase the applicability of our method, we apply it to two real-world data sets, highlighting its usefulness. Additionally, we examine the relationship between the concept of matching safety and the more widely studied concept of matching rank, finding that our method can be viewed as a risk-averse variant of matching rank. This connection enables us to derive upper bounds on matching safety in terms of matching rank. Finally, we investigate how the individual's decision-making style influences the outcome of the matching process, discovering that different strategies often yield different stable matches. In an effort to address this issue, we propose a new objective function known as the "regret of mismatching" to measure the suboptimal matches that an individual's decision-making style might produce. Our analysis reveals that calculating this regret in an exact manner is computationally complex, but we can apply a more efficient method based on the bipartite graph matching problem to yield a practically effective solution. Our method can be used to find a compromise between different individual styles by minimizing their regret of mismatching. In particular, we apply this method to the data sets mentioned earlier to yield stable matches that are more robust against variations in individual styles. In summary, our paper explores the proposal selection problem with multiple proposals and develops a range of efficient methods to solve it, including matching safety and regret of mismatching. These methods are found to be practically effective in both exact and approximate settings. In addition to these methods, we also compare the single-proposal model with the multiple-proposal model, discovering that different individual styles often yield different stable matches. The increasing use of deep neural networks in control systems poses significant challenges in terms of validation and verification. The primary obstacle stems from a lack of well-established methods for validating learning-based control systems. This study aims to address this issue by introducing a novel validation approach for neural networks. Our approach builds on the fundamental property that control systems must convert initial conditions into unique outputs, and that any system violating this property is considered non-valid. Inspired by the concept of image approximations, we have developed a new method to assess neural networks' validity by examining their initial state uniqueness property. This method involves creating surrogate models by perturbing the real network and checking if the resulting models produce distinct outputs. Our results indicate that a certain percentage of these surrogate models, known as 'good' models, should confirm the original network's uniqueness, ensuring its validity. We have also demonstrated that these 'good' models congregate in a region known as the 'valid set'. By testing these 'good' models, we have successfully validated the neural network. This approach allows us to quantify the validation rate of the neural network, which represents the proportion of valid models out of all tested models. Our experiments have shown that the valid set can be approximated by sampling a large number of surrogate models. Additionally, we establish a link between the problem of solving the normalization problem for T tours of size k vertices in O(Tk^3) time to resolve the problem of finding a T-MWIS in general, with similar constraints. This unexpected result leads us to devise a new algorithm specifically created to tackle the T-MWIS problem with t > 1, with the capability of being adapted into a polynomial-time approximation algorithm for solving the problem of finding an MWIS in general, with similar constraints. Recent advances in artificial neural networks (ANNs) have led to remarkable progress in visual understanding, and these models are increasingly used in practical applications. However, there is still a significant gap in understanding how humans and ANNs differ in their visual abilities. A key challenge lies in developing methods that can effectively compare human and machine performance. Our research focuses on this question, and we found that severe image transformation tasks, which measure how much an image is altered while still allowing for its recognition, offer valuable insights into this issue. When tested with these tasks, ANNs outperformed humans, and interestingly, the results varied depending on whether the tasks involved shifting image parts or adjusting their overall distribution. Our findings indicate that ANNs are better equipped for handling transformations that are easily managed by their hierarchical pooling mechanisms, whereas humans struggle with these changes. On the other hand, ANNs underperformed humans when tested with non-uniform image distribution transformations, suggesting that human visual capabilities transcend the limitations imposed by the current design of ANN architectures. Our research implies that ANNs can learn to match human visual abilities if the range of possible transformations is properly considered in their design. By employing a novel method that models human behavior using a dynamic memory mechanism, we were able to develop a more comprehensive understanding of human visual processing and identify areas where ANNs can improve their performance. Redshifts of distant objects are crucial for cosmology, astrophysics, and planet science, and their measurement is error-prone. To address this issue, we've developed the High-z Sudoku algorithm, a robust method for identifying the most reliable redshift ranges in follow-up spectroscopic observations, particularly for millimeter-wavelength objects. This technique has a high false positive rate of 10% without any prior information about the object's nature. The analysis focuses on a sample of 31 objects primarily discovered by the REDCOAL, NOEMA, and IRAM 30m Telescopes. The sample's redshift distribution shows a range from 1.2 to 6.0, with a median redshift of z = 2.7. The High-z Sudoku algorithm identified 21 objects with likely redshifts, and their distribution spans from z = 1.3 to z = 5.9, with a median redshift of z = 2.7. The algorithm's results are consistent with the original redshift estimates for 19 objects, and it missed one expected redshift, while two objects had uncertain redshifts. The analysis suggests that the High-z Sudoku algorithm is a reliable tool for identifying the most likely redshift ranges in future follow-up observations, particularly for millimeter-wavelength objects. The algorithm's results are mainly based on the presence of molecular lines like HCN(4-3), HCO+(1-0)-1, and HCN/(HCO+) (1-0) in the millimeter range. The algorithm's success is mainly due to the presence of strong self-absorption features in the line profiles, which are more common in high-redshift objects. This breakthrough offers significant potential for reducing the computational costs associated with generating and completing temporal knowledge graphs. Research on Kerr-lens mode-locked lasers has grown, leading to high-peak-power femtosecond lasers with low noise and tunability across ultraviolet to infrared wavelengths. These lasers have numerous applications including non-linear spectroscopy, microscopy, seeding for amplifiers, and generating supercontinua and few-cycle pulses. Achieving stable Kerr-lens mode-locking in high-peak-power lasers is challenging due to mechanical and thermal issues that must be carefully managed. The complex physical processes involved in mode-locking make it hard to predict performance based on published data. We present an intuitive geometrical analysis of Kerr-lens mode-locking that considers critical factors like beam overlap, apodization of the beam, and Kerr-lens threshold. This approach provides a clear understanding of the interplay between these elements and helps in optimizing a laser for mode-locking. We validate our method by applying it to various lasers with different geometries and beam profiles, enabling us to identify the key factors that contribute to mode-locking and offering a valuable tool for researchers working with high-peak-power ultrafast lasers. Using our approach, we have successfully identified the essential criteria for mode-locking in our experimental setup, enabling us to achieve stable Kerr-lens mode-locking at high powers. Notably, we have obtained stable single-mode operation at 400 mW of average power with a low time-bandwidth product of 0.40, yielding a record-breaking pulse duration of low enough that the frequency bandwidth cannot further narrow the pulse. Online Federated Learning (OFLL) holds great promise for securely and efficiently training complex machine learning models across numerous devices, thereby avoiding data centralization. Asynchronous OFLL allows individual devices to train at their own pace based on locally cached data, yet the Nonlinear Regression application typically requires data exchange between devices. Consequently, asynchronous OFLL tends to get stuck in a situation where devices wait for data exchange. This paper tackles the challenge of implementing asynchronous OFLL for Nonlinear Regression through a novel asynchronous framework. The proposed framework enhances convergence by leveraging periodic aggregation and decoupling model and parameter updates. Additionally, differential privacy is integrated into the framework via local regularization and gradient clipping. The experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a balance between convergence, accuracy, and computation and communication efficiency, particularly at low regularization levels. The effective approach is that of "learning as one, optimizing as many." The proposed framework's performance is comparable to synchronous and parallel federated learning methods, and significantly outperforms existing asynchronous frameworks. We focus on using node representation for predicting links in sparse networks, particularly those involving recommendation systems. Current node representation methods, such as node2vec, are well-suited for dense networks but don't perform well in sparse networks due to their discursive nature. In response, we've developed SSNE, a new node representation framework tailored for sparse networks and compatible with recommendation systems. SSNE efficiently predicts links on public datasets, outperforming existing approaches. For instance, it improves link prediction accuracy in Amazon Product Graph by 122.7%, while reducing overall processing time compared to node2vec. SSNE achieves this performance through a local sampling strategy, which generates node representations more relevant to recommendation tasks. Additionally, SSNE's extended version, SSNE+, further enhances its capabilities by leveraging knowledge to improve its predictions. SSNE and SSNE+ demonstrate their potential on public Amazon Product Graph and YouTube Product Graph datasets, paving the way for future research in sparse networks. Our model also assumes a proportional distribution of new infections among uninfected individuals. The model we've created is an extension of standard COVID-19 models found in the literature, which are typically deterministic and assume infections occur uniformly. In contrast, our stochastic model provides a more accurate representation of real-world COVID-19 data, which exhibits significant variability. Using COVID-19 data from the United States, we've estimated key parameters for our model, including daily growth rates, hospitalization risks, and the distribution of infections among uninfected individuals. Recent studies of the Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance (ISGMR) in a range of nuclei have highlighted the resonance's sensitivity to nearby quadrupole excitations.  To investigate further,  the ISGMR was investigated in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si using (α, α′) cross sections measured at multiple energies around the resonance peak.  To account for coupling effects between the ISGMR and the Isoscalar Giant Quadrupole Resonance (ISGQR), a new theoretical approach was developed.  Results showed that when this coupling was considered, a more accurate estimate of the ISGMR energy could be achieved, with observed energies of 18.1 MeV for $^{24}$Mg and 21.2 MeV for $^{28}$Si.  Additionally, coupling had a minimal effect on the width of the ISGMR, with experimental widths of 1.9 MeV for $^{24}$Mg and 3.3 MeV for $^{28}$Si.  This new approach is expected to be applicable to a broad range of nuclei.  Comparisons with theoretical estimates based on the Random Phase Approximation (RPA) suggested that the method could be used to provide valuable insights into the underlying structure of nuclei.  Further research will investigate the application of this method to a wider range of nuclei.  Ultimately, this work has significant implications for the study of nuclear structure, with potential applications in a range of fields.  To confirm this, experimental and theoretical studies of the ISGMR in a range of nuclei are now being undertaken.  Initial results of these studies are expected to be published in the near future. In recommender systems, users' purchase decisions are often influenced by various underlying motivations such as desire, cost savings, or social status. By taking these intentions into consideration, product recommendations can be tailored not just to users, but also to their specific goals. However, current recommendation approaches only adjust for users and ignore their motivations. To address this gap, we propose a novel technique that simultaneously models users and their underlying purposes. Our approach involves a two-part framework: (1) a deep learning model that infers users' short-term purposes through their purchase history, and (2) a purpose-inference model that determines the long-term intentions underlying users' successive purchases over multiple time steps. Experimental results on real-world data from an e-commerce platform show that this goal-aware framework improves both short-term and long-term recommendation accuracy, particularly in scenarios involving many users and items. This research delves into the theoretical aspects of estimating a low-rank matrix drawn from a specific distribution that accounts for non-homogeneous noise levels in different sub-matrices. By applying a specific decomposition, we have established a sharp spectral guarantee and a sharp phase transition for this estimation problem, which generalizes a previously established result for the homogeneous noise setting. Moreover, we have derived an optimal recovery condition for which exact matrix recovery is possible under Gaussian noise conditions. Additionally, we have provided lower and upper bounds for the mean squared error in this setting. Furthermore, we have established a sharp phase transition for the estimation of mixed-rank matrices under specific conditions. Finally, we have outlined potential directions for future research. The results of this research have been substantiated through numerical simulations. Moreover, we have applied these theoretical findings to a relevant real-world problem, such as single-cell RNA-seq data. A related software package, named HetTensor, has been developed for this research, which utilizes an alternating minimization optimization technique to estimate the low-rank matrix under heterogeneous noise conditions. This software package can be downloaded from GitHub under the open-source Apache-2.0 license agreement. The inherent topological model (ITM) of quantum mechanics describes how quantum systems function based solely on their observables, without reference to symmetry. This paper presents a novel feature of ITM that is unlikely apparent in quantum theories emphasizing symmetry: its ability to derive a unitary basis from a given set of observables without necessitating any underlying symmetry. A general approach to this problem is outlined, along with specific applications to particular types of quantum systems. A notable example is the study of a finite quantum spin-j system, where a known relation between its Hamiltonian and observables is utilized to construct the ITM unitary basis. A detailed comparison between the proposed method and a recent topological model for quantum spin chains, due to E. Berg, is also presented. ITM provides a universal framework for topological quantum computing that is independent of symmetry, making the described method a significant one. Furthermore, this work showcases the ITM computing potential by demonstrating its application to a challenging problem, the Simon's problem, which has significant implications in quantum computing. A detailed computation of the ITM Hamiltonian for this problem is presented, along with a proof that its eigenvalues follow a specific pattern. This research highlights the robustness and inherent characteristics of quantum systems described by ITM. A broader perspective on these findings is also offered. 2021 by the authors. The rapid progression of quantum information systems is driven by advancements in microkelvin technology, particularly in developing large-scale superconducting qubit systems. These advancements are heavily reliant on the availability of substantial, millikelvin cooling resources. This document outlines a large-scale cryogenic system currently under development at Fermilab, which aims to provide a 100-mK cooling capacity in a transportable box, potentially expanding to even colder temperatures with the incorporation of additional helium-3 cryogenics. This innovative cooling architecture will integrate three key components: a 1-K pre-cooling system, a 100-mK cryogenic refrigerator, and a 10-mK insert for record-low temperatures. The proliferation of geotagged images on social media platforms like Flickr, Google Street View, and OpenStreetMap provides a wealth of information on the characteristics of urban environments, encompassing historical, cultural, and geographical data. This extensive collection presents a challenge, however, as manually extracting and aggregating the tags from the vast number of geotagged images is a daunting task. To address this issue, this study proposes a solution: leveraging the collective wisdom of the social media crowd through a voting-based algorithm to automatically generate geotagged tags for urban spaces. This method, dubbed VALUE, utilizes a map-reduction technique to combine local votes, thereby facilitating the efficient extraction of valuable information from social media platforms. An evaluation of the algorithm's performance using two cities as test cases demonstrated its effectiveness in accurately identifying relevant tags. Additionally, value provides users with a customizable interface for exploring the algorithm's output, thereby enabling users to tailor the results to their specific needs. This research aims to shed light on the potential of social media platforms for urban research and development by providing a tool for collecting and understanding the collective perceptions of urban residents. In seismic reflectivity inversion, the primary objective is to derive a seismic image from recorded data via an inversion process, often constrained by the characteristics of wave propagation and the physical attributes of the subsurface. Advanced NLP models heavily rely on part-of-speech tags, which are often inaccurate in older texts. We propose a new Set-Valued Machine Learning approach to accurately assign sets of possible tags to sentences from historical documents, taking into account the inherent uncertainty in tagging outdated language. This method enables better handling of ambiguous words and words with changing meanings over time. We developed a Set-Valued POS tagger for Middle English and Early Modern English texts, achieving improved results with error rates well under 10% for the EMT corpus, compared to over 30% for modern languages and up to 60% for EMT when using traditional single-value models. This breakthrough marks the first time error rates for EMT have surpassed those of modern languages. Furthermore, our innovative technique can be applied to any language part-of-speech tagging task without any modifications. We are making our code and trained models available to the public, aiming to lay the groundwork for a new generation of uncertain data handling in NLP, which in turn could lead to significant advancements in the field. The models and source code can be found at https://github.com/CLPER/set-valued-pot. Additionally, the dependent repository for processing the EMT corpus can be found at https://github.com/CLPER/EMT.

Recently, models combining vision and language have achieved significant progress, 
with particular advancements in image-text models such as CLIP. However, there 
remains a limitation in image-text models, which is that they often fail to capture 
critical information when images and text assets are not closely associated. To 
overcome this challenge, we introduce VT-CLIP, a pre-trained model that utilizes 
visual cues to guide text comprehension, which is achieved by training it on datasets 
featuring visual-guided text phenomena. We also develop a new dataset called 
Apples-and-oranges, which is used to evaluate the effectiveness of VT-CLIP in image-text 
comparisons and in concept associations. Experiments have demonstrated VT-CLIP's 
superior performance in image-text matches and concept associations compared to 
existing models, and it has also outperformed other baseline models in zero-shot and 
few-shot tracking tasks. Moreover, VT-CLIP's capability to extract and localize text 
features from images has enabled it to outperform other visual-language models in 
visual-directed visual tracking tasks. We have also made publicly available VT-CLIP, 
along with new datasets, at https://github.com/AllanZhou/human-eye-model.

The adoption of artificial intelligence in digital pathology and radiology healthcare has accelerated, with a focus on incorporating machine learning models into clinical practice to enhance diagnosis and treatment accuracy. Despite this progress, there are ongoing technical and data management hurdles to overcome, particularly when it comes to complying with relevant healthcare standards. To address these challenges, we have developed highdicom, an open-source Python library, to streamline the conversion of image analysis results and machine learning model outputs into standardized digital formats. This project utilizes the DICOM data model to facilitate data exchange, with a focus on image acquisition and analysis. Highdicom enables users to create standard digital representations of annotated images and machine learning model outputs, as well as XML files for configuration and input/output purposes. To demonstrate its usability, we have applied highdicom to a digital pathology dataset and a CT scan dataset, and made the associated code and datasets available for public viewing on GitHub. This work has been completed with the goal of enabling the seamless adoption of machine learning models in clinical settings and pathology image analysis. Highdicom is available for public download at https://github.com/Stanford-STARR/highdicom. Rendered HTML documentation can be accessed at http://htmlpreview.github.com/htmldoc/highdicom. This work has been supported by the National Cancer Institute (1R01CA196421) and the National Institute of Mental Health (1R01MH114979). The source code for highdicom is released under the Apache 2.0 license. The associated datasets are released under the data.govvulcan terms of service. The increasing accessibility of genomic data through cost-effective sequencing technologies has led to a surge in available genomic information, making unsupervised learning techniques essential for extracting valuable insights from these datasets. Our study focuses on developing an effective, unsupervised deep learning framework that captures intricate features within genomic data, enhancing our comprehension of low-level DNA patterns. This method demonstrates the capacity to derive meaningful characteristics from sequencing data automatically, mirroring the process by which the human genome develops primary gene regulatory elements. Furthermore, it enables the identification of overrepresented patterns (ORFs) in both artificial and real-world genomic data, as well as artificial sequences modeled after the latter. Our results show that the proposed model achieves a high recall of 0.2369 (or 23.69\%) when applied to the DREAM5 track1 dataset, surpassing the best performing model in the track. Additionally, we successfully applied our method to the ENCODE regulome track to identify novel regions exhibiting a strong enrichment of transcription factor binding sites. Our technique also performed favorably in a comparative evaluation of methods that use deep learning for genomic character extraction. It outperformed existing techniques in identifying coding and non-coding regions within artificial genomic sequences. Overall, the proposed method offers a valuable tool for analyzing genomic data, allowing researchers to visualize ORFs at varying scales, from the genomic level to a focused 1-kb window, showcasing their widespread presence across the human genome. This study is a continuation of a discussion on enhanced conservation theories for complex fluid dynamics equations as modeled by Navier-Stokes equations. A broader class of equations, including rotation-invariant and Galilean-invariant models, is considered, allowing for systematic derivation of global energy inequalities for both incompressible and compressible fluids. By extending the framework established in a previous study for incompressible fluids, a new theory is developed, which includes a conservation theorem for the averaged kinetic energy in compressible fluids. Although the general approach remains the same, several significant technical differences arise between incompressible and compressible fluids, prompting a separate investigation. A key innovation here is the application of a novel integration by parts procedure, which overcomes a significant obstacle in the compressible case, allowing for a broader understanding of enhanced conservation principles. Numerical examples are also provided to illustrate the validity and utility of these theories. Consider a simple undirected graph $G$ with edge-labeling. We say that an edge-labeling is sequential on a subset of vertices $V'$ if it satisfies the following conditions:
- All vertices in $V'$ have degree at most one.
- For each edge in $G$, either both or neither vertices belong to $V'$.
- The edges in $V'$ are sequentially arranged.

We establish a lower bound for selecting vertices in $G$ to apply sequential edge-labeling. For a graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and edges, (n-1)/2 < m ≤ n, we show that either a subset of vertices with degree at most one contains all edges in $G$, or a subset of vertices with degree at most one contains edges that are sequentially arranged. This result generalizes to a larger family of graphs called $H$-graphs. Furthermore, for bipartite graphs, we find that bipartite graphs with more than three vertices have a higher selection ratio than non-bipartite graphs. Finally, we show that bipartite graphs with certain properties have a similar selection ratio to complete graphs of the same order. This result leads to several open questions. For instance, is it true that bipartite complete graphs have a higher selection ratio than non-bipartite graphs. And, is it true that bipartite graphs with more than three vertices have a higher selection ratio than complete bipartite graphs of the same order. This research showcases an advanced approach to managing and characterizing tunnel couplings essential for the development of quantum processors. We've also found that the quantum tunneling of particles through a large insulating gap is not hindered by the presence of a Coulomb blockade. This research provides a significant step forward in the control and characterization of tunnel couplings, a crucial component for the design of quantum processors capable of processing multiple qubits. We've demonstrated the ability to both identify and manipulate these couplings, including their ability to operate at sub-Kelvin temperatures even when a quantum dot is in a blockade state. This control over tunnel couplings is a key aspect of quantum processing architectures relying on quantum tunneling. Although the standard theory only applies to perfect fluids, it has been expanded to accommodate realistic models of gas through relaxation limits. However, the theory for weak solutions is still limited due to the involvement of non-physical phantom states. To address this issue, entropic discontinuities are used, combining the theoretical benefits of conservation law-based shock waves with the physical properties of interacting gas states. We aim to develop a novel view generation technique that captures and maintains depth information in a single real-world image. Traditional methods fail to generalize due to hardware limitations and changing scene depths. In contrast, generative models like Perpetual View Generation (PVG), can generate novel views from a single image, but they lack the accuracy and generalizability required for reliable results. To overcome these challenges, we integrate a learned depth estimation model into a generative model framework by modifying a conditional diffusion model to incorporate both RGB and depth inputs. Experimental results demonstrate our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art PVG methods, achieving significant improvements in view generation quality and overall performance. Notably, our approach also surpasses that of synthetic datasets in terms of novel view generation quality. When evaluated on the challenging KITTI dataset, our method outperforms existing baselines, setting a new benchmark for reliable single-view generation. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/wheresthecad/DiffDreamer. With further advancements in monocular depth estimation, our approach has the potential to significantly contribute to the field of PVG. The model's integration of RGB and depth inputs enables novel view generation even when depth information is unavailable. To this end, we also propose a novel evaluation metric that accounts for view generation quality and depth accuracy, demonstrating the model's ability to generate realistic novel views with accurate depth maps. The model's performance on the KITTI dataset shows promising results, with novel view generation quality scores comparable to those of PVG methods. Notably, our approach outperforms existing baselines in novel view generation quality, setting a new benchmark for the KITTI dataset. The model's performance highlights the importance of accurate depth estimation in the model's training pipeline, emphasizing the need for further generalizable depth estimation techniques. To this end, we also investigate the impact of various depth estimation methods on the model's performance, providing valuable insights for the PVG community. The integration of robotic technology in ultrasound imaging has shown improved reliability and enhanced point-of-care diagnostics, particularly in scoliosis detection and screening. This study compares the accuracy of robotic and manual scanning techniques in measuring curvature and vertebral rotation through ultrasound imaging. To assess reliability, robotic and manual scanning approaches are applied multiple times (six to eight times) while maintaining fixation on the same spinous process. Curvature and vertebral rotation measurements are recorded and statistical analysis performed to establish intra and inter observer correlations. Results show that robotic scanning achieves high levels of reliability, demonstrating strong correlations with curvature (r=0.91) and vertebral rotation (r=0.83) measurements. Furthermore, robotic scanning exhibits comparable reliability to manual scanning, with no statistically significant differences in curvature (p=0.22) and vertebral rotation (p=0.56) measurements. This study's findings support the use of robotic scanning as a reliable method for scoliosis assessment via ultrasound imaging. Key advantages of robotic scanning include its ability to enhance consistency and objectivity in measurement outcomes, particularly in the presence of user fatigue. This technology's potential to streamline scoliosis detection and screening could significantly contribute to point-of-care diagnostics, especially in the emergency department and other healthcare settings. Future studies should focus on developing algorithms that integrate robotic scanning with clinical decision support systems to optimize patient care. This research could lead to various applications of ultrasound imaging in the assessment and screening of scoliosis, ultimately enabling more efficient and reliable diagnostic care. This paper outlines our solution for the MedNet 2020 challenge, which focused on generating synthetic speech durations. We compared several methods, including a complex regression approach based on linguistic features and a simpler duration embedding method. Our results showed that a median-based duration estimation technique provided the most accurate outcomes. Therefore, we combined this method with a median-based approach to refine duration estimates. A non-parametric technique was used to model the conditional distribution of true durations given the synthetic ones. We trained this model using the training corpus and applied it to test data, achieving a relatively low duration accuracy of 78.03%. Subsequent density-based duration adjustments yielded significant improvements, increasing density-based accuracy to 91.89%. Ultimately, our solution for the MedNet 2020 challenge achieved an F-score of 0.8127, ranking it 4th out of 26 submissions. Further analysis revealed that our solution effectively handled speech types, tonalities, and rate categories, even with limited training data. Therefore, we believe this solution can be effectively applied to various networks and databases, especially those with limited resources. Identifying and categorizing online content as hate speech is a critical task, 
especially with the rise of social media as a primary platform for global
communication. Accurate hate speech detection is crucial for preventing the
spread of harmful content and reducing its negative impact on social relations. 
Previous studies have employed machine learning models, which often rely on
sequential models due to the importance of word order in language understanding. 
Notably, these models require extensive data and rely on existing annotations, 
limiting their applicability to new domains and social media platforms. 
In contrast, feature selection-based methods integrate feature extraction more
coherently and offer greater adaptability across various domains. 
Our proposed model, FS-LSTM, combines a feature selection method with an
LSTM architecture, demonstrating superior performance in hate speech identification 
on three datasets, including one social media dataset. 
The FS-LSTM model surpasses existing standards with a high F1 score of 0.903 
on the Twitter-Hate dataset and outperforms the baseline F1 score by 2.2% 
and 1.9% on the SemEval2016-Task5 and Twitter-Hate datasets, 
as well as the social media dataset by 8.4%, 5.8%, and 4.6% respectively. 
The model's adaptability is further highlighted by its ability to identify hate
speech on Arabic and Spanish text with minimal adjustments, showcasing its
potential for real-world applications on multiple domains. 
Our model's source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/tonyramr/FS-LSTM. 
The paper also includes a model's reliability assessment through a
Blind-Test analysis. The study's findings are of value to researchers and
practitioners working in related fields, while the code's accessibility
facilitates its reproduction by other scholars. The model's performance on
arbitrary datasets can be examined through a web-based demo at
https://hatespeechlstm.herokuapp.com. The model's performance is also
evaluated on other datasets in a later related study at
https://www.semanticscholar.com/abstract/Blind-Text-Blind-Tim: A Large-Scale-Open-Dataset-for-Text-Blindness-Recognition/7b3b4b3b.

Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) models have achieved superior performance in natural language processing tasks. However, their inherent parallel processing structure, combining short and long-range features, hinders the exchange of information between parallel pathways, hindering rapid feature sharing. This inefficiency can be addressed by revisiting the MIMO model's architecture, specifically the design of its multiple branches, to enhance both intra and inter-pathway interactions. To this end, we investigate the MIMO model's properties and introduce two novel network configurations that facilitate shared features among different lengths of computational paths. Our experimental results on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that these new architectures significantly outperform the current state-of-the-art models, including MIMO models with improved feature sharing and other top-tier models. Moreover, their performance is comparable to that of lightweight self-attention mechanisms. This study is the first to dissect the MIMO model's properties and offer a new understanding of its architecture through the lens of feature sharing. We have made our code available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ai-research-MEGA/MIMO-Feature-Sharing. Efficient non-equilibrium Green's functions allow for the accurate description of complex electronic transport across metal-molecule interfaces, thanks to their ability to model quantum-coherent devices. However, in such analysis, density functional theory calculations face significant challenges when dealing with the morphology of molecules that cannot be simplified to a single junction, such as those with multiple contacts. This article presents a groundbreaking approach to address this limitation by combining the results of separate, self-contained calculations representing individual contact points with an innovative multi-point mapping technique to merge these results into a cohesive, molecule-embedded density. This embedded density serves as the foundation for constructing an accurate, multi-port transport model. To demonstrate the versatility of our proposed method, we successfully apply it to various molecules with diverse bonding configurations to the contacts and highlight the distinct features of their electronic transport properties. Overall, our developed scheme facilitates the efficient simulation of complex electronic transport in a broad range of quantum-coherent devices supported by molecules. Its versatility extends to the modeling of nano-structures featuring molecules with multiple attachment points, which could potentially lead to the identification of novel molecular electronic transport modes, such as quantum conductive switches, in the future. In any given graph, a subset of vertices called a resolving set can pinpoint every vertex by calculating their distances to at least one vertex from the resolving set. The minimum size of such a resolving set is known as the dimension of the graph, and a set of vertices with the smallest possible dimension is called a minimum resolving set. A parameterized problem related to finding minimum resolving sets is defined as follows: given an input graph and a parameter set which can be either the size of the minimum resolving set or a specific type of vertex subset called a feedback vertex set, determine if there exists a vertex subset with a maximum size equal to the parameter that is also a minimum resolving set. This problem turns out to be solvable in a specific time complexity class for certain structural graph types but intractable for more complex graph structures even with a specific type of input where the minimum resolving set has a limited size. A similar problem related to finding the maximum possible dimension when considering a vertex subset with at most the parameter set's given size is the input, also known as the Maximum Dimension on a p-set problem, is defined as follows: given an input graph and a parameter set which can be either the size of the minimum resolving set or a specific type of vertex subset called a feedback vertex set, determine if there exists a vertex subset with a maximum size equal to the parameter that has the maximum possible dimension. This problem turns out to be solvable in a specific time complexity class for certain structural graph types but intractable for more complex graph structures even with a specific type of input. A related problem where the goal is to find the maximum possible dimension when considering a vertex subset with at most the parameter set's given size and also contains at least one vertex from the input, also known as the Maximum Dimension on an H-covering p-set problem, is defined as follows: given an input graph and a parameter set which can be either the size of the minimum resolving set or a specific type of vertex subset called a feedback vertex set, determine if there exists a vertex subset with a maximum size equal to the parameter that has the maximum possible dimension. This paper introduces a topology-based structure, referred to as the $\mathcal P$-directed space, derived from the weak topology, and identifies suitable conditions for both open and closed maps in this context. Furthermore, it explores the interrelation of these maps with Hausdorff properties in $\mathcal P$-directed spaces and discusses various examples of mappings within these spaces. Moreover, a subcategory of $\mathcal P$-directed spaces, denoted as $\mathcal P\mathfrak D$, is established and investigates the mapping properties within $\mathcal P\mathfrak D$. Finally, this paper delves into the interplay between the closed map property and other essential characteristics of directed spaces in $\mathcal P\mathfrak D$. It is also shown that the closed map property can be utilized to extend and generalize various results in directed spaces to the category of $\mathcal P$-directed spaces. These results, in turn, are applied to the study of Hausdorff properties in $\mathcal P$-directed spaces. It is demonstrated that a specific closed map property, analogous to the $\mathcal P$-closed map property, is instrumental in the generalization of these results. Deep neural network classification systems for critical applications like medical image processing rely heavily on high-quality annotations, but these rely on imperfect labels which can lead to significant errors in prediction. The problem becomes more complex in medical settings due to the lack of reliable experts in specific fields. Existing methods focus on improving robustness against noisy labels but often discard unreliable annotations instead, which can be disastrous if valuable data is discarded, like valuable medical image data. To solve this, a new method called the Bayesian Statistics Guided Label Rejuvenation Mechanism (BSLRM) is proposed to identify and correct noisy labels based on the reliability of annotations. By using a Bayesian neural network to predict image classes, BSLRM assesses annotation reliability by measuring how well it aligns with the neural network's predictions, and selects the most reliable label based on posterior probability. As a result, BSLRM achieves significant improvements over state-of-the-art approaches, including an improved accuracy of 8% and 10.7% over naive and data reweighing baselines, respectively, in medical image classification. Evaluation on three public medical image datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of BSLRM in mitigating label noise. To promote its practical use, a 3-step medical image classification workflow incorporating BSLRM is provided to help practitioners handle real-world label noise in medical image classification tasks. This study examines the properties of an interpolation projector in a real Hilbert space, establishing a measure of its norm that is relevant in various practical scenarios. Specifically, we analyze the situation where the norm of the interpolation projector is constrained by the sum of the norms of certain vector combinations and error vectors, tied to the performance of an optimal estimator. Our findings also include conditions under which this constraint becomes an equality. The relationships between these results and the minimum mean square error (MSE) criterion are further explored and illustrated with a relevant example from the literature. The outcome indicates that, in certain circumstances, utilizing an MSE-constrained projector can yield equivalent performance to its unconstrained counterpart. In formal specifications, relations are often used to describe system states and their changes over time.  Relational definitions allow for the formal treatment of concepts like functions, inverses, and iteratives, playing a crucial role in organizing a logic-based specification.  Despite their importance, traditional methods for handling relations as a fundamental data type are not always suitable for handling timed relations effectively.  This paper presents an innovative approach, building upon the HOL logic to incorporate timed relations as a fundamental, definable data type, similar to functions and propositions.  A timed relation's truth-value is determined by a pair of ordinary relations, one applicable at a specific time point and the other covering the entire timeline.  This groundbreaking, purely axiomatic, and sound foundation enables a complete recasting of the HOL logic, resulting in a new system dubbed HOL_Timed.  A comprehensive proof that the system is consistent has been provided.  This work has been successfully implemented in HOL Light, an interactive proof assistant.  A substantial collection of formal specifications in this new language has been developed, primarily in functional and imperative styles, to demonstrate its power and versatility.  It has been successfully used to model and verify key data structures, including queues, priority queues, and deques, as well as network routing algorithms, particularly Dijkstra's and A\* algorithms.  This new foundation has also facilitated a novel approach to non-interference, a classic security property, allowing for a concise and elegant formalization. In this regime, previously chiral Majorana edge modes become Majorana fermions that encircle minigaps in a crystalline structure. While this regime destroys the semi-metallic nature and produces a gap in the spectrum, it leaves the chiral mode at the Fermi level unchanged. This leads to two types of fractional Chern insulators, one controlled by the golden ratio and the other by its inverse value. This development presents opportunities to study the interplay between a topological effect, a periodic change in magnetic field, and the emergence of a gap in a crystalline structure. Overampling, a form of data augmentation by generating extra examples, is used to enhance machine learning resilience. Unlike traditional methods that only change input data, this technique also alters outputs to improve model generalization. The development of new overampling methods based on search algorithms has led to a range of options being added to the existing toolbox. This study evaluates the effectiveness of 16 overampling techniques, including 4 that modify outputs and 12 that utilize optimization methods, in a multi-class text classification task. The results show that a simple output modification method surpasses more complex methods in terms of performance. The investigation also reveals that using a combination of methods can further improve the outcome. The findings suggest that overampling should be based on specific problem and data characteristics, and not as a one-size-fits-all solution. The proposed output modification methods can be used as an alternative to method of record search, and are more computationally efficient. The research also indicates that overampling can be problem and data dependent, and therefore it is recommended to apply it only after the initial model has been trained. This study examines the relationship between local TV news coverage of the U.S. COVID pandemic and its impact on death rates, considering different demographics and newscast topics, using data from a major broadcast news source and COVID case and death statistics from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The Sinkhorn algorithm is widely used to solve the Schrödinger problem, a key task in optimal transport theory. It's considered to yield an approximate solution, but the convergence rate wasn't well-documented until recent studies established a $O(1/k)$ convergence rate in simplified settings. However, these simplified settings exclude cases where costs have varying signs. Even when such situations arise, recent research demonstrated that the algorithm can't converge to a solution in all cases, leading us to question the convergence rate in these scenarios. Our contribution is to establish that, in cases where the Schrödinger problem has no solution, the Sinkhorn algorithm still converges to a critical point, which we show to be unstable under perturbations. Furthermore, we provide evidence suggesting that, when dealing with costs having no varying signs, the algorithm can still converge to a solution, which we believe to be the case due to the problem having a solution in such scenarios. An additional issue arises when dealing with costs having a single minimum value, in which case the algorithm is shown to converge linearly. We provide supporting numerical examples and apply our findings to a real-world traffic management problem. We believe our research to be the first to document the algorithm's behavior in cases where the Schrödinger problem has no solution, which we hope will contribute to the development of more effective and efficient algorithms for solving optimal transport problems in such scenarios. An accompanying software package is available at https://github.com/alexkurland/sinkhorn_unbalanced_uniqueness, which includes the code used in our research, as well as a traffic management demonstration. We have also applied our research to the field of quantum chemistry, specifically to the problem of matrix product states, in which we believe our research to be the first to document the algorithm's behavior in such scenarios. A new approach called field-split facilitation has emerged as a faster and more efficient method for solving partial differential equations. However, the FC methods' advantage in CPU time decreased as the time step increased due to the overhead costs of the FC algorithms. The study suggests that using FC methods can significantly improve the convergence rates, but the choice of time step should be guided by a balance between convergence rates and CPU time. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of future research in reducing the overhead costs of the FC algorithms. Presently, robots lack a standardized way of interacting with humans, with each interaction tailored to a specific situation, which can lead to confusion when general rules apply. To address this, we developed a learning-based approach that enables robots to adapt human expectations of consistency in communication. To achieve this, we created a mixed-initiative task that leverages a shared-autonomy interface to guide a robot's path through an environment. By splitting this task into multiple steps, we found that humans tend to expect more predictable behavior from the robot as the task progresses from the initial planning to the final execution stage. These prompts were initially tested in a collaborative driving simulation and demonstrated to improve human-robot collaboration. To facilitate adoption, we developed an open-source prompt library that can be easily integrated into existing autonomous systems, enabling them to communicate more effectively with humans. Current methods rely on either global mapping techniques that can be computationally expensive in dynamic environments or sequential mapping techniques that may not suit tasks requiring global awareness. The source code for HiTMap is publicly available and can be easily integrated into existing mapping and localization algorithms. This work introduces a novel approach called Term Relevance Response (TRR), which directly responds with relevant terms rather than entire documents, effectively customizing rankings to suit conversational entity retrieval needs. To assess its efficacy, a new benchmark has been established and performance benchmarks set for both traditional and TRR-based methods. The results show that TRR outperforms traditional ranking techniques in context-aware NER and achieves state-of-the-art results with only partial contextual information. The initial x-ray absorption near edge spectra (XANES) process involves a series of sequential electron group transitions driven by incrementally increasing photon absorption, influencing the overall absorption pattern. This study presents a novel model that characterizes these electron groups and their individual transitions to generate a theoretical cumulated absorption curve. A simplified approximation is applied to transform the complex Wigner 3-j symbols expression, facilitating direct adjustments to the generated XANES profiles in line with experimental changes in x-ray energy flux and residual atomic density, without altering the underlying transition energies. These calculations are based on average residence times of electron groups and chaperone regulation mechanisms following full occupation of the ground state. They also account for the chaperone efficiency in facilitating additional transitions and its impact on final absorption levels. This rate-of-electron-group model is applied to the case of the tryptophan indole chromophore, providing insights into its relaxation dynamics and regulation by chaperones. These findings are particularly relevant for non-linear XANES investigations at high fluences, and the proposed model can be extended to analyze other complex biological molecules. A computer program implementing this model, written in Python, is available for download at https://github.com/roberts-soft-matter-and-bio-physics/xaness_rate_ofElectronGroupModel. A corresponding Python program using the PyLinX framework for non-linear XANES simulations is provided at https://github.com/roberts-soft-matter-and-bio-physics/PyLinX_rateOfElectronGroupModel. A supplementary website containing the model and supporting materials is accessible via https://www.myu.ac.uk/physics/staff/roberts/index.html. Using this model, simulations of XANES spectra matching experimental findings have been achieved for cytochrome c and myoglobin. These results indicate that the model is applicable to a broad range of biological molecules. Further research is necessary to determine the model's potential for chaperone characterization. This paper introduces MuMuPy, a program for computing the interaction cross-sections of dimuonium states with real nuclei. Dimuonium, composed of a bound electron and muon pair, can potentially bind to atomic matter through interaction with photons and the exchange of electrons and muons. MuMuPy's accuracy has been verified by comparing its calculations of dimuonium-photon interactions in a hydrogen atom to existing theoretical models. It then employed these interactions to estimate dimuonium production within hydrogen-like atom nuclei via photon-photon scattering and photon elastic scattering. MuMuPy calculates interactions at the Born level, supplementing these findings with a discussion of potential relativistic corrections in dimuonium physics. Furthermore, the program examines the implications of dimuonium production in hydrogen-like atom nuclei for experimental searches, highlighting the potential significance of the European XFEL and Facility for Antiproton-to-Hadron Collisions experiments in dimuonium research. We introduce a new approach called Spartan, which learns to represent signals with varying sparsity using a differentiable method. We formulate signal representation as a problem that minimizes a cost function subject to constraints on the sparsity level. We reformulate this as a problem of optimal transportation between a signal's density distribution and its target sparsity distribution, resulting in a differentiable method for signal representation. We show that Spartan can be applied to convolutional and recurrent neural networks and can be used as a layer in existing neural networks. As of our knowledge cutoff in May 2021, this survey aims to deliver an up-to-date overview of the state-of-the-art in evolving graph embedding.
