Robotic manipulation tasks are often complicated by vision obstacles. An effective approach to navigating these challenges involves using an eye-in-hand camera attached to a robotic manipulator, which can be positioned remotely. However, directly translating image data from a single camera pose to other poses can be problematic due to changing viewpoints. Traditional methods for adjusting eye-in-hand camera positions often rely on prior knowledge or involve time-consuming trial-and-error processes. In contrast, we propose a new learning-based technique that can automatically adjust eye-in-hand camera positions in real-time, even when there's no prior knowledge available. This method leverages a single image and exploits the relationships between 3D objects and their viewpoints, which are learned through a network called Multi-View Regressor. By training this network, we can pinpoint the target pose with the desired view, and then use geometric transformations to calculate the required camera movements. Our algorithm can handle complex and irregular 3D objects, and can adjust camera positions in as little as 20 milliseconds. In our experiments, we found that our method outperforms existing approaches in terms of target accuracy, with an average error reduction of over 30%. We introduce an innovative approach that synergizes semi-supervised training of an end-to-end automatic speech recognition system with inter-domain loss. Our method begins by leveraging a pre-trained speech-ngram model to generate pseudo labels for unsupervised inter-domain loss. To minimize domain gaps, we employ CycleGAN to match the distribution of speech transcriptions, thereby optimizing the inter-domain loss. The pseudo labels generated are sequentially refined throughout the training process, initially enhancing early-stage unsupervised training, before being replaced by real labels in later stages of supervised training. Our experiments on the WSJ, Librispeech, and TED-LIUM datasets reveal significant improvements in word error rate, with gains of 2.1%, 2.5%, and 1.5% observed respectively, when compared to models trained with only pre-trained Gaussian-Basis Autoencoders as pre-training components. Notably, our method demonstrates superior performance when compared to other advanced inter-domain loss techniques. The source code is publicly available on GitHub.

The evaluation of student performance in writing is a crucial aspect of assessment. However, the labor-intensive process of manual evaluation by experts hampers widespread adoption of this method. Automated assessment of essays faces challenges due to the inherent complexities and variability of language, as well as formatting and content disparities that must be factored into consideration during evaluation. This research explores the feasibility of utilizing transformer-based language models, such as BERT and RoBERTa, to improve automated essay assessment by incorporating style and diversity considerations into the evaluation process. By adapting a suitable objective function, the models successfully distinguish essays by the same author with different writing styles, as well as identify unique content. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the models' evaluations correlate with human assessments, providing promising results for the use of transformer-based models as a reliable and efficient solution for automated essay assessment. This approach also enables the development of a versatile tool capable of accommodating various evaluation criteria and styles, including multiple experts' marking guidelines. The findings demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing automated assessment techniques, providing a more accurate and robust solution. This research is part of a larger project, 'Transformers in Education', a comprehensive investigation into the applications of transformer-based models in educational settings, including their use in automated essay assessment, semantic search, and as a proxy for human annotation in understanding student written language. This work can be accessed on our project website at https://transformers-in-education.github.io/. Additionally, the code and data used in this research are publicly available at https://github.com/DeepLogicAcademy/AutomatedEssayAssessment. Overall, the method presents a significant advancement in automated essay assessment, offering a promising solution for experts to utilize as a primary or supplementary tool in their evaluation processes. Nevertheless, the decision to adopt this method should be made with caution, taking into account the inherent biases that may be present in the training data. This limitation is pertinent to all machine learning models, underscoring the necessity for experts to scrutinize the data used in the training process. Moreover, future research should seek to rectify the potential drawbacks of the proposed approach. One potential direction for future investigation is to explore the feasibility of using transformer-based language models in conjunction with other established automated essay assessment techniques, such as vector representation models, to mitigate the possible biases that may affect the results. This combination of methods could lead to a more robust and reliable automated essay assessment system. We introduce the Box Re-Ranking (BRR) module, which suppresses false positives and enhances domain adaptation for pedestrian detection. Operating on detection box embeddings, BRR assigns confidence scores and masks to each box, differentiating valid pedestrians from other objects. A unsupervised box-ranking loss is proposed, optimizing a single-scale box distribution to prevent false positive suppression. Experiments on the Citypersons dataset show BRR improves detection rates by 5.8% and 3.5% respectively on Domain 2 and Domain 3 relative to a baseline. Further, an end-to-end model combining BRR and a deep domain confusion architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming the baseline by 7.7% and 4.7% on Domain 2 and Domain 3 respectively. The model also surpasses a strong fully-supervised model by 0.7% and 0.4% on Domain 2 and Domain 3 respectively. The detailed analysis confirms BRR's effectiveness in domain adaptation and its ability to outperform a fully-supervised model. The code and models are available at https://github.com/kuangul/box-re-ranking. Our primary objective is to examine how throwing motions are perceived when the point of release does not match the expected standard. To achieve this, we created a simulation tool that mimics human perception and used it to create faux throws by modifying the radial velocity of throwing gestures at different points near the end of the motion, particularly where the point of release is typically observed. These modifications resulted in novel throwing motions where the point of release appears uncertain. In a human study involving both expert and novice participants, we analyzed their responses to these faux throws and found that novice participants frequently identified the point of release incorrectly, whereas expert participants rarely did. Furthermore, we discovered that the point of release influences not only the perceived throwing technique but also the perceived throwing force. In cases where the point of release appears early, participants tend to perceive a forceful throw; in cases where the point of release appears late, participants tend to perceive a feeble throw. Our research suggests that the standard point of release is an essential cue for inferring throwing techniques and forces. In order to improve the realism of virtual simulations and evaluate human throwing abilities effectively, we recommend incorporating diverse points of release, particularly near the end of the motion, to reflect the variability of actual throwing motions. Such variability can also facilitate the detection of faux throws and increase their overall plausibility. Ultimately, our research highlights the importance of considering the complexities of human motor assessment. A new software, the Binding Energy Assessment Platform, was developed to help determine binding energies, even when experimental data is limited. The performance of text classification models can be compromised by the presence of labels that are missing, misformatted, or redundant. To overcome this challenge, we suggest an approach based on the SIBYL variant by Leakey et al. at NeurIPS'20. This method involves a linear classifier that utilizes a direction towards the hyperplane normal to accurately identify the most likely class label for each given instance. Our modifications to this SIBYL variant aim to enhance its adaptability to classification tasks, particularly when there are multiple labels involved. Additionally, we propose an improved version of the SIBYL variant that leverages an adaptive normal classifier, which is trained to optimize performance on a sample-by-sample basis. Our theoretical analysis confirms that the SIBYL variant is robust against dataset perturbations and also meets the requirements of being well-calibrated and reliable. To further validate the efficacy of our SIBYL variant modifications, we conducted experiments on 16 diverse datasets and observed significant performance improvements, with average accuracy increasing by 6% and macro-F1 scoring increased by 5%. Our study demonstrates that the SIBYL variant is a versatile and effective approach that can be applied to a broad spectrum of classification tasks. You can access the code for our study at https://github.com/ashishg16/sibylvariant_text_classification. Our study's findings are consistent with those presented at IJCAI'21 by Leakey et al. where SIBYL was shown to be effective for question answering tasks. To date, SIBYL has been successfully applied to both text classification and question answering tasks. Nevertheless, a notable limitation of SIBYL is its dependence on an existing set of clean labels which is often not a feasible requirement in real-world scenarios. To address this concern, we conducted a series of experiments aimed at identifying which features contribute the most to the robustness of SIBYL. Our analysis reveals that SIBYL's performance is most susceptible to errors when dealing with 'Definition' features. Consequently, we developed a novel variant of SIBYL, referred to as SIBYL-D, which is specifically designed to mitigate the negative impact of 'Definition' related errors. SIBYL-D achieves this by leveraging an additional direction towards the hyperplane normal that is orthogonal to the 'Definition' direction. In the realm of few-shot learning, traditional methods often rely on hand-coded metrics or labels obtained from supplementary data. This research delves into meta-learning techniques that enable an algorithm to automatically acquire a linear transformation to minimize a specified distance metric between a support set prototype and a query set points, with both the distance metric and target prototype being automatically determined. We demonstrate that by employing a specific type of optimization known as gradient descent, these parameters, which we term'meta-parameters,' converge to a first-order stationary point under certain conditions related to the geometry of the data. Notably, these conditions are data-dependent and unrelated to the choice of distance metric or target point, making them data-based. Furthermore, our findings show that these meta-parameters can be successfully applied across multiple, disparate metrics, and that a two-stage optimization process can yield results comparable to state-of-the-art methods on tasks involving prototypical networks, while operating independently of the chosen metrics. We apply this method to several tasks including multi-task learning, using the KNN classifier on unlabeled data, and transfer learning, and demonstrate its effectiveness on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The code for this research can be found at https://github.com/alexkcenter/demonstrable_meta_learning.

Developing small language models is a high priority area of study, driven by successful applications such as text classification and machine translation. Recent advances in large pre-trained language models, combined with transfer learning and knowledge distillation techniques, have made small models feasible. This paper investigates the potential of leveraging large, high-performance models trained on low-resource datasets for small model development, particularly in languages with limited data. We examine the effects of transferring models trained on richer datasets into a smaller context and vice versa, as well as the use of knowledge distillation techniques. We compare the stability of quantization and distillation methods to reduce model size, focusing on English-Swedish and English-Finnish machine translation tasks using Transformer models. We analyze the performance degradation of various models when subjected to adversarial attacks and evaluate their robustness using metrics such as BLEU scores. We find that knowledge distillation improves translation quality, with sequential distillation yielding better results than concurrent distillation. However, we also observe that small model performance varies significantly depending on the method and source model, suggesting that certain techniques and source models are more effective than others. This study's findings highlight the importance of considering multiple approaches to develop small models, particularly in challenging low-resource settings where translation quality can differ substantially depending on the method and source model used. We make our code and models available to support reproducibility. We believe our results have significant implications for developing small MT models, particularly in contexts where data is scarce and resources are limited. We recommend that model developers carefully evaluate the trade-offs of using various methods and source models to develop small models, given the performance variability we have identified. This variability also underscores the need for more research on developing small models in extremely challenging settings such as languages with extremely limited translation data available. We believe our study's insights can be extended to other NLP tasks and related NLP challenges like model compression, transfer learning, and developing small models in resource-constrained settings. We plan to extend our study to other related areas in the future. These limitations become more pronounced in the realm of zero-shot speech-to-speech translation that doesn't rely on language pairs during training. This study investigates the feasibility of extending existing speech translation models to facilitate zero-shot speech-to-speech translation by leveraging only speech-to-text models as a intermediate step. Our experiments involve using multilingual speech-to-text models as a middle ground to demonstrate zero-shot speech-to-speech translation capabilities. In particular, speech-to-text models for 8 languages were used in conjunction with speech-to-speech models for 6 languages, resulting in an average sequence-level BLEU score of 9.94 for the English source language, a 2.66x improvement over direct speech-to-speech translations. Our analysis reveals that the effectiveness of speech-to-text intermediaries in zero-shot speech-to-speech translations depends heavily on speech-to-speech model performance, with better target speech quality resulting in improved translations. This study provides the first systematic exploration of zero-shot speech-to-speech translation capabilities through speech-to-text intermediaries, shedding light on their potential role in facilitating this challenging task. The proposed approach opens up new avenues for research in zero-shot speech-to-speech translation. This work was possibly the first to demonstrate zero-shot speech-to-speech translation capabilities. Our experimental results show that the existing method can achieve a reasonable zero-shot speech-to-speech translation performance, with a maximum BLEU score improvement of 1.43x and an average increase of 0.83x, respectively. Our analysis reveals that the existing method is influenced by several factors, including speech quality, data parallelism, and source speech characteristics. Machine learning's growing influence on software engineering practices suggests a promising future for automated machine learning as a service. However, the current state of the art falls short of fully incorporating domain knowledge, hindering the quality of predictions and explanations sought by software engineers. To bridge this gap, this paper outlines a framework for integrating domain knowledge into machine learning algorithms. The proposed approach involves three key steps: first, using literature mining to gather domain knowledge in the form of rule learning; second, converting this knowledge into Semantic Web Ontology format; and third, modifying a base classifier to incorporate the optimized knowledge. The feasibility of this framework is demonstrated through a practical example and a prototype developed for the Eclipse platform. An empirical study comparing baseline results to the proposed approach confirms its effectiveness, indicating improved prediction accuracy with proper tuning of hyperparameters. The widespread coronavirus pandemic has prompted medical institutions to rely on supplementary hospital capacities, straining the healthcare system. Extracting and analyzing medical image data, including chest X-rays and CT scans, has played a pivotal role in global research on the disease. Specifically, automatic detection and segmentation of pulmonary lesions in these images have been critical for diagnosing COVID-19. Notably, existing research on these tasks relies heavily on datasets annotated by experienced medical professionals, which can be both time-consuming and costly. Moreover, standard lesion annotations often involve comprehensive spatial and visual information, further exacerbating the problem. This paper seeks to address these challenges through the development of a novel framework that utilizes weakly supervised learning to create unbiased lesion localization and segmentation models for pulmonary lesions in COVID-19, without requiring comprehensive spatial and visual information or time-consuming annotation processes. By employing a small number of bounding box annotations, the proposed framework trains a COVID-19 lesion detection model that can adapt to various imaging data without bias. Furthermore, by leveraging the dense prediction property of U-Net, the proposed framework extends the detection model to perform precise lesion segmentation, effectively creating a versatile detection and segmentation pipeline for pulmonary lesions in COVID-19 and other diseases. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed framework's exceptional performance, outpacing state-of-the-art models by a significant margin, with a 6.0% improvement in F1 score and 2.4% improvement in Dice similarity coefficient, respectively. The proposed framework's effectiveness is further validated through experiments using annotated datasets of lung CT scans from patients with pulmonary tuberculosis, demonstrating its ability to create unbiased lesion detection and segmentation models. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification play a crucial role in diagnosing and treating spinal disorders. This process can be challenging due to the lack of distinctive features, especially in the thoracic region. To address this issue, we propose a novel method that leverages our previous work, vertebrae $L_2$ norm regression, in conjunction with spine rectification and anatomically-constrained optimization. By integrating these techniques, we achieve significant improvements in both localization and identification, resulting in state-of-the-art performance. To this end, we introduce Spine-OSE, a method that adapts the optimization framework to extract the spinal curve and align vertebrae labels in non-collinear positions, thereby minimizing the distance between these points. This method also constrains optimization within anatomically plausible regions, ensuring that optimization does not deviate from the spinal curve. To further enhance performance, we introduce a multi-resolution approach, using $L_2$ norm regression at different resolutions to refine vertebral landmarks. Experiments on large public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of Spine-OSE, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both localization and identification. To facilitate widespread adoption, we provide source code and model repositories for easy access. This work represents a major step towards fully automatic spinal CT segmentation. This study has been selected for oral presentation at MICCAI 2021. The related code and models can be found on our GitHub repository https://github.com/autospine/Spine-OSE. The dataset used in this study can be found on https://www.cadiz-spine.org/. Our CT-Anatomy dataset, comprising 1,000 spinal CTs, is currently under preparation for public release.
